div.p: When at last I had been set free, either wholly or in great part, from the labours of advocacy and from my senatorial duties, I betook myself once more, Brutus, chiefly at your urging, to those studies which, though kept alive in my mind, had been laid aside as the times demanded and after a long interval interrupted; and since the system and discipline of all the arts that bear upon the right conduct of life are comprehended in the pursuit of wisdom which we call philosophy, I thought it my task to set this forth in the literature of our own tongue — not because philosophy could not be grasped through Greek writings and Greek teachers, but because it has always been my judgement that our countrymen have either discovered everything for themselves more wisely than the Greeks, or else have improved upon what they received from them, at least in those matters which they had judged worthy of their labour.

Neoptolemus, indeed, in Ennius says that he must needs philosophize, but only a little, for he had no liking for it altogether. As for me, Brutus, I judge that I must philosophize — for what better thing can I do, especially now that I have nothing to do? — but not a little, like him. For it is difficult in philosophy to know a few things and not either most or all; since neither can a few things be chosen except out of many, nor will one who has grasped a few not pursue the rest with the same zeal.

What, Brutus, am I to think is the reason why, though we are composed of mind and body, an art has been sought for the tending and care of the body, and its usefulness consecrated to the discovery of the immortal gods, while the medicine of the mind has been neither so longed for before it was found, nor so cultivated after it became known, nor so welcome and approved by many — by more, even, suspected and hated? Is it because we judge the heaviness and pain of the body with the mind, but do not feel with the body the sickness of the mind? So it comes to pass that the mind judges of itself at the very time when that by which the judging is done is itself diseased.

In many respects, Brutus, I am wont to admire the talents and virtues of our countrymen, but most of all in those studies which, sought very late, they carried over into this state from Greece. For when, from the very rise of the city, by the kingly institutions, and in part also by the laws, the auspices, the ceremonies, the assemblies, the rights of appeal, the council of the fathers, the ordering of horse and foot, the whole art of war had been divinely established, then an admirable advance was made, and an incredible course toward every excellence, once the state was freed from kingly domination. Nor indeed is this the place to speak of the morals and institutions of our ancestors, and of the discipline and ordering of the state; these things have been treated by me with sufficient care in other places, and most of all in those six books which I wrote On the Commonwealth.

This fifth day, Brutus, will make an end of the Tusculan Disputations, on which day was disputed by us that matter which of all you most approve. For I have perceived, both from that book which you wrote to me with the greatest care, and from many of your conversations, that it pleases you well that virtue is of itself sufficient for living happily. And although this is difficult to prove, on account of the so various and so many torments of fortune, it is yet of such a kind that one must labour at it, that it may the more easily be proved. For there is nothing of all that is handled in philosophy which is spoken more weightily or more magnificently.

For in our manners and the ordering of our lives, and in our domestic and family affairs, we certainly maintain ourselves both better and more handsomely; and as for the commonwealth, our ancestors assuredly governed it by better institutions and laws. What need I say of the art of war? In this our countrymen have prevailed greatly by valour, and still more by discipline. And as for those things which they attained by nature rather than by letters, they are not to be compared either with Greece or with any nation whatever. For where was there ever in any people such gravity, such steadfastness, such greatness of soul, such honesty and good faith, such virtue of every kind so excellent, as to bear comparison with our forefathers?

Yet still, in a busy life, and a soldier's, such as Neoptolemus then led, even a few things often profit much and bear fruit — if not so great as can be reaped from philosophy entire, yet at least such fruits as in some part now and then set us free from desire or from distress or from fear. Thus from that disputation lately held by me at my Tusculan villa there seemed to come a great contempt of death, which avails not a little to free the mind from fear. For he who fears that which cannot be avoided can in no way live with a tranquil mind; but he who fears not death — not only because one must die, but also because death holds nothing to be dreaded — has secured for himself a great defence toward a happy life.

But if Nature had begotten us such that we could behold and discern her very self, and accomplish the course of life under that best of guides, there would assuredly have been no reason for anyone to seek for method and instruction. As it is, she has given us tiny sparks, which we, swiftly perverted by bad habits and opinions, so quench that nowhere does the light of Nature appear. For there are in our minds the inborn seeds of the virtues, which, if they were allowed to grow up, Nature herself would lead us to a happy life. But now, as soon as we are brought forth into the light and taken up, we are at once involved in all manner of depravity and in the utmost perversity of opinions, so that we seem to have sucked in error almost with our nurse's milk. And when we are given back to our parents, then handed over to our teachers, then we are so steeped in various errors that truth gives way to vanity, and Nature herself to confirmed opinion.

But in this place, as I consider the studies of learning, many reasons indeed occur to me why these too should seem to have been fetched from elsewhere, and not only sought, but even preserved and cultivated. For there was almost within their sight, surpassing in wisdom and renown, Pythagoras, who was in Italy in the same times in which Lucius Brutus freed his country — that glorious founder of your nobility. And since the teaching of Pythagoras flowed far and wide, it seems to me to have penetrated into this state; and this is both probable by conjecture and indicated even by certain traces. For who is there who would think, when Greece flourished in Italy with its most powerful and greatest cities — that which was called Magna Graecia — and when in these, first the name of Pythagoras himself, then afterward that of the Pythagoreans, was so great, that the ears of our countrymen were closed to their most learned utterances?

For since that cause impelled those who first betook themselves to the study of philosophy, that, all things else being set aside, they should bestow themselves wholly upon the inquiry after the best state of life, surely it was in the hope of living happily that they placed so great a care and labour upon that study. And if by them virtue has been discovered and perfected, and if there is enough of protection in virtue toward living happily, who is there who would not judge that the work of philosophizing was both gloriously laid down by them and gloriously taken up by us? But if virtue, subjected to various and uncertain chances, is the handmaid of fortune, and is not of such great strength as to guard itself, I fear that we must seem to lean toward the hope of living happily not so much by trust in virtue as by making of vows.

In learning, and in every branch of letters, Greece surpassed us; and it was easy to win where there was no resistance. For while among the Greeks the most ancient class of the learned is that of the poets — since Homer and Hesiod lived before the founding of Rome, and Archilochus in the reign of Romulus — we Romans took up poetry later. It was about five hundred and ten years after the founding of Rome that Livius produced a play, in the consulship of Gaius Claudius, son of Caecus, and Marcus Tuditanus, one year before the birth of Ennius. He was older than Plautus and Naevius. Late, then, were poets either known or welcomed among us. Yet it stands in the Origines that guests at banquets were once accustomed to sing to the flute of the virtues of famous men; but that no honour attached to this calling is shown by a speech of Cato's, in which he cast it up as a reproach to Marcus Nobilior that he had taken poets with him into his province — and that consul had, as we know, taken Ennius into Aetolia. The less honour, then, that was paid to poets, the less were such pursuits cultivated; nor, even so, where men of great genius arose in that field,

And yet I am not unaware that many will be eager to argue against me; which I could in no way avoid, save by writing nothing at all. For if my speeches, which I wished to be approved by the judgement of the multitude — for that faculty is a popular one, and the effect of eloquence is the approval of those who hear — but if there were found some few who would praise nothing save what they were confident they could imitate, who set themselves the same limit in their hope of speaking well as in their power, and who, overwhelmed by the abundance of thoughts and of words, declared they preferred leanness and hunger to richness and plenty — whence had arisen that breed of \"Attic\" speakers, unknown to those very men who professed to follow it, men who have now fallen silent, laughed almost out of the Forum itself:

The poets, too, come in addition, who, when they have made a great show of learning and wisdom, are heard, read, learned by heart, and cling deep within our minds. And when to these there has come, as it were, a kind of greatest master, the people, and the whole multitude consenting on every side to vices, then we are plainly infected with the depravity of opinions and revolt from Nature; so that those seem to us to have seen best the power of Nature who have judged nothing better for man, nothing more to be sought, nothing more excellent than honours, commands, and the glory that comes from the people. Toward this every best man is carried, and, seeking that true honour which Nature above all desires, he busies himself in the utmost emptiness, and pursues no eminent likeness of virtue, but a shadowy image of glory. For glory is a certain solid and well-defined thing, not shadowy: it is the agreeing praise of good men, the uncorrupted voice of those who judge rightly of excellent virtue; it answers back to virtue as an echo; and because it is generally the companion of right deeds, it is not to be spurned by good men.

Nay, I even think that, on account of admiration for the Pythagoreans, King Numa too was reckoned a Pythagorean by later men. For since they knew the teaching and institutions of Pythagoras, and had received from their ancestors the equity and wisdom of that king, but were ignorant of the ages and times on account of antiquity, they believed that he who excelled in wisdom had been a hearer of Pythagoras. And of conjecture, indeed, thus far. But although many traces of the Pythagoreans could be collected, we shall yet use a few, since that is not our business at this time. For since those men are said to have been wont to deliver certain precepts somewhat secretly in songs, and to lead their minds from the intensity of their thoughts to tranquillity by song and the lyre, Cato, a most weighty authority, said in his Origins that this was the custom among our ancestors at banquets — that in turn those who reclined should sing to the pipe the praises and virtues of famous men; from which it is plain that there were then both melodies set to the sounds of voices and songs.

For my part, considering with myself those chances by which fortune has vehemently exercised me, I begin sometimes to distrust this opinion and to dread the weakness and fragility of the human race. For I fear lest Nature, when she had given us infirm bodies, and had added to them both incurable diseases and intolerable pains, gave us also minds both attuned to the pains of the body and, separately, entangled in their own anguishes and troubles.

did they fall short of the renown of the Greeks. Do we suppose that, had it been counted to the credit of Fabius, a man of the noblest birth, that he could paint, we too should not have had many a Polyclitus and Parrhasius? Honour nourishes the arts, and all men are kindled to their pursuits by glory, while those that are everywhere held in disesteem lie always neglected. The Greeks judged the highest cultivation to lie in the music of strings and voices; and so Epaminondas, in my judgement the foremost man of Greece, is said to have played excellently on the lyre, while Themistocles, some years before, when he declined the lyre at a banquet, was thought the more unschooled. Thus in Greece musicians flourished, and all learned the art, nor was anyone who was ignorant of it thought fully accomplished in his education.

what shall we think will happen, when we see that we can least of all now use the people for our helper, as we used it before? For philosophy is content with few judges, of its own purpose shunning the multitude, by it both suspected and hated — so that, should anyone wish to revile philosophy entire, he might do it with the people on his side, or, should he attempt to assail that school which we above all follow, he might find great support in the doctrines of the other philosophers. But I have answered the revilers of philosophy entire in my Hortensius; and as for what was to be said on behalf of the Academy, I think it has been set out accurately enough in the four books of my Academica. Yet so far am I from being unwilling that anything be written against me, that I should even most earnestly wish it. For in Greece itself philosophy would never have been held in such honour, had it not flourished by the contentions and disagreements of the most learned men.

But that other thing, which wishes to be its imitator — popular fame, rash and inconsiderate, and generally the praiser of faults and vices — corrupts the form and beauty of glory by a pretence of honour. By which blindness men, when they desired even certain glorious things and yet knew not where or of what kind they were, have, some of them, utterly overthrown their own states, others slain themselves. And these, indeed, seeking the best, are deceived not so much in their will as in the error of their course. What of those who are carried away by greed of money, by the lust of pleasures, and whose minds are so disordered that they are not far from madness — which befalls all the foolish? Is no cure to be applied to them? Is it because the sicknesses of the mind do less harm than those of the body, or because bodies can be cured, while for minds there is no medicine?

Although the Twelve Tables too declare this — that it was even then the custom to compose a song; which, lest it might be done to another's injury, they sanctioned by law. Nor indeed is that no argument of a cultured time, that to the gods' couches and to the magistrates' banquets the lyre plays — which was proper to that discipline of which I speak. To me, indeed, even the song of Appius Caecus, which Panaetius greatly praises in a certain letter that is addressed to Quintus Tubero, seems Pythagorean. There are many things, too, in our institutions drawn from them; which I pass over, lest those things which we are thought to have ourselves discovered should seem to have been learned from elsewhere.

But in this I chastise myself, that from the softness of others, and perhaps of my own, I judge of the strength of virtue, not from virtue itself. For she — if only there is any virtue, which doubt your uncle, Brutus, removed — has beneath her all things that can befall a man, and, despising them, contemns human chances, and, free of all fault, thinks nothing pertains to her save herself. But we, both magnifying by fear all adversities as they come, and by mourning those that are present, choose to condemn the nature of things rather than our own error.

Among them geometry was held in the highest honour, and so nothing was more illustrious than the mathematicians; but we have fixed the bounds of this art by its usefulness in measuring and reckoning. On the other hand we were quick to embrace the orator — at first not a learned one, but apt for speaking, and afterwards learned as well. For it is recorded that Galba, Africanus, and Laelius were men of learning, and that Cato, who was older than they, was eager for it; then came Lepidus, Carbo, and the Gracchi, and after them such great men down to our own age that little or nothing was yielded to the Greeks. Philosophy has lain neglected until this very day and has had no light shed on it by Latin letters; it is for us to illumine and awaken it, so that, if while engaged in affairs we were of some service to our fellow citizens, we may serve them also, if we can, in our leisure.

Wherefore I exhort all who can do it to wrest from now-languishing Greece the glory of this kind too, and to carry it over into this city of ours — even as our ancestors, by their zeal and diligence, carried over all the rest that was worth seeking. And whereas the glory of orators, brought up from humble beginnings to its height, has now reached the point — as Nature brings about in nearly all things — of growing old, and seems destined in a short time to come to nothing, let philosophy take its birth in our Latin letters from these times of ours; let us assist it, and let us suffer ourselves to be refuted and confuted. This those bear with an ill grace who are, as it were, bound and consecrated to certain fixed and predetermined opinions, and are constrained by that necessity to defend, for consistency's sake, even what they are not wont to approve. But we, who follow what is probable and cannot advance beyond what presents itself as likely to the truth, are ready both to refute without obstinacy and to be refuted without anger.

But the diseases of the mind are both more pernicious and more numerous than those of the body. For these very ones are hateful, because they belong to the mind and trouble it; and the sick mind, as Ennius says, is ever wandering, can neither bear nor endure, and never ceases to desire. By which two diseases — to pass over the rest — distress and desire, what, pray, can be heavier in the body? But how can it be proved that the mind cannot heal itself, when the mind itself discovered the very medicine of the body; when for the healing of bodies the bodies themselves and Nature avail much, and not all who have suffered themselves to be cured forthwith recover, whereas minds, which have wished to be healed and have obeyed the precepts of the wise, are without any doubt made whole?

But that my discourse may return to its purpose — in how short a time how many and how great poets, and what orators too, arose! So that it readily appears that our countrymen could attain everything, as soon as they began to wish it. But of the other studies we shall speak in another place, if there be need, and have often spoken. The study of wisdom, indeed, is old among us; yet before the age of Laelius and Scipio I find none whom I could name by name. In whose youth I see that the Stoic Diogenes and the Academic Carneades were sent as envoys to the senate by the Athenians; who, since they had never touched any part of public affairs, and since the one was a Cyrenaean, the other a Babylonian, would surely never have been roused from their schools nor chosen for that office, had there not been in certain leading men of those times zeal for learning. Who, while they committed other things to writing — some the civil law, some their own speeches, some the monuments of their ancestors — pursued this most ample of all the arts, the discipline of living well, by their life rather than by their writings.

But of this fault, and of our other vices and sins, all correction is to be sought from philosophy. Into whose bosom, since from the first times of our age our will and zeal impelled us, now, tossed by these gravest chances in a great storm, we have fled for refuge to the same harbour from which we had set out. O philosophy, guide of life, O searcher-out of virtue and expeller of vices! What, not only we, but the life of men altogether, could have been without you? You gave birth to cities; you called together scattered men into the fellowship of life; you joined them among themselves, first by dwellings, then by marriages, then by the communion of letters and of speech; you were the inventor of laws, you the teacher of morals and of discipline. To you we flee, from you we seek help, to you we entrust ourselves — as before in great part, so now wholly and entire. But one day well and according to your precepts spent is to be preferred to a sinning immortality.

And here we must labour the more diligently because many Latin books are now said to have been written thoughtlessly by men who were indeed excellent but not sufficiently learned. For it may well happen that a man thinks rightly and yet cannot express what he thinks with elegance; but for anyone to commit his reflections to writing who can neither arrange them, nor set them in a clear light, nor allure his reader with any charm, is the mark of a man squandering without restraint both his leisure and his letters. And so such writers read their own books only with their own circle, and no one touches them save those who wish to be granted the same licence of writing for themselves. Wherefore, if by our industry we have brought some credit to oratory, with far greater zeal we shall open up the springs of philosophy, from which those gifts also flowed.

But if these studies are once brought over to our countrymen, we shall not even have need of the Greek libraries, in which the multitude of books is boundless, owing to the multitude of those who have written. For the same things are said by many, and so they have crammed their books with everything. This will happen with ours too, if more flock to these studies. But let us, if we can, stir up those who, being liberally educated, and joining to it an elegance of discourse, philosophize by method and by rule.

There is assuredly a medicine of the mind: philosophy. Whose aid is not, as in diseases of the body, to be sought from without; but with all our resources and strength we must labour that we may be able to heal ourselves. Although, concerning philosophy in general — how greatly it is both to be sought and cultivated — enough, as I think, has been said in the Hortensius. And on the greatest matters I have since left off neither disputing nor writing. In these books are set forth those things which were disputed by me with my friends at Tusculum. But since in the two former books death and pain were treated, the third day of disputation will make up this third volume.

And so of that true and elegant philosophy, which, drawn from Socrates, has hitherto persisted among the Peripatetics, and likewise among the Stoics who say the same things in another manner, while the Academics decided their controversies, there are scarcely any, or very few, Latin monuments — whether on account of the greatness of the matters and the engagements of men, or even because they did not think those things could be approved by the unskilled; while meanwhile, those keeping silence, Gaius Amafinius came forward as a speaker, whose books being published, the multitude was stirred and betook itself to that teaching above all — whether because it was very easy to know, or because they were enticed by the soft allurements of pleasure, or even because, nothing better having been brought forward, they held to what there was.

Whose aid, then, should we use rather than yours, you who both bestowed on us tranquillity of life and took away the terror of death? And philosophy, indeed, is so far from being praised in proportion as it has deserved of the life of men, that by most it is neglected, by many even reviled. Does anyone dare to revile the parent of life, and to stain himself with this parricide, and to be so impiously ungrateful as to accuse her whom he ought to revere, even if he had been less able to grasp her? But this, as I think, is the error, and this the darkness poured over the minds of the unlearned — that they cannot look back so far, and do not think that those by whom the life of men was first equipped were philosophers.

But just as Aristotle, a man of the highest genius, knowledge, and copiousness, when he was moved by the renown of the rhetorician Isocrates, began to teach young men to speak as well, and to join prudence with eloquence, so it is my resolve neither to lay aside my former zeal for speaking, and at the same time to occupy myself with this greater and richer art. For I have always judged that to be the perfect philosophy which can discourse copiously and with ornament upon the greatest questions; and I have given myself to this exercise so earnestly that I have even ventured to hold disputations in the manner of the Greek schools. So lately, after your departure, when several of my friends were with me at my Tusculan villa, I made trial of what I could do in that kind. For as I formerly declaimed upon set cases — and no one did so longer than I — so this is now my old man's declamation. I would bid them propose whatever subject any of them wished to hear discussed; and upon that, either sitting or walking, I would dispute.

For there is a certain sort of men who wish to be called philosophers, of whom there are said to be a great many books in Latin — which for my part I do not despise, seeing that I have never read them; but since those very men who write them profess that they write neither with clear distinction nor with orderly arrangement nor with elegance nor with ornament, I neglect a reading that gives no pleasure. For what these men of that school say and think, no one even moderately learned is ignorant of. Wherefore, since they themselves take no pains as to how they say it, why they should be read — except by those of like mind among themselves — I do not understand.

For when we had gone down into our Academy, the day being now inclined toward the afternoon, I asked one of those present for a theme to discourse upon. Then the matter went thus: It seems to me that distress can befall the wise man. — What, the other disturbances of the mind too — fears, lusts, fits of anger? For these are about the kind of thing which the Greeks call pathē. I might call them \"diseases,\" and that word would be word for word; but it would not suit our usage. For pity, envy, exultation, joy — all these the Greeks call diseases, motions of a mind not obedient to reason; but these same motions of an agitated mind we should rightly, I think, call \"disturbances,\" and \"diseases\" not very customarily — unless something else seems to you. — To me, indeed, that way.

After Amafinius, moreover, many rivals of the same system, having written much, occupied all Italy; and the very thing which is the greatest argument that those things are not said with subtlety — that they are both so easily learned by heart and approved by the unlearned — this they think to be the firm foundation of their teaching. But let each defend what he thinks; for judgements are free: we shall keep to our practice, and, bound by the laws of no single school, which in philosophy we must necessarily obey, we shall always inquire what is most probable in any matter. Which, as I have often done elsewhere, so lately at Tusculum I pursued with zeal. And so, the disputations of three days being set forth, the fourth day is concluded in this book. For when we had gone down into the lower walk — which we had done likewise on the former days — the matter went thus: Let anyone say, if he will, on what subject he wishes to dispute.

Which thing, though we see it to be most ancient, we yet confess the name to be recent. For who can deny that wisdom itself is ancient, not only in fact, but even in name? Which, by the knowledge of things divine and human, and of the beginnings and causes of each thing, won this most beautiful name among the ancients. And so both those Seven, who were held and named by the Greeks sophoi, by our countrymen sapientes (wise men), and, many ages before, Lycurgus, in whose times Homer too is reported to have lived, before this city was founded, and already in the heroic ages Ulysses and Nestor — we have heard that these both were and were held wise men.

And so I have set down in the same number of books the five days' disputations — schools, as the Greeks call them. The manner was this: when the one who wished to hear had said what seemed to him to be the case, then I would argue against it. For this, as you know, is the old and Socratic method of disputing against another's opinion; for so, Socrates thought, what was most like the truth could most easily be found out. But that our disputations may be set forth the more conveniently, I shall present them as though the thing were being enacted, not narrated. Thus, then, the opening will arise. — Death seems to me to be an evil.

For, just as Plato and the rest of the Socratics, and after them those who proceeded from these, are read by all, even by such as do not approve those teachings or do not pursue them most earnestly, whereas Epicurus and Metrodorus are taken up by scarcely anyone but their own followers, so these Latin writers are read by those alone who think their doctrines rightly stated. But to us it seems that whatever is committed to writing ought to be commended to the reading of all the learned; nor, if we ourselves are less able to attain to this, do we therefore feel that it should the less be done.

Do you think, then, that these can befall the wise man? — I think so entirely. — Then that vaunted wisdom is not to be reckoned of great worth, if indeed it differs not much from madness. — What? Does every commotion of the mind seem to you madness? — Not to me alone; but, as I am often wont to wonder at, I find it so seemed to our ancestors too, many ages before Socrates, from whom all this philosophy that concerns life and morals has flowed. — In what way, pray? — Because the word \"insanity\" signifies a sickness and disease of the mind, that is, unsoundness and a sick mind, which they called insanity.

It does not seem to me that the wise man can be free of every disturbance of the mind. — Of distress, indeed, he seemed, in yesterday's disputation, unless perhaps you assented to me for the occasion's sake. — By no means; for your discourse was excellently approved by me. — You do not, then, think that distress befalls the wise man? — I do not think it at all. — And yet, if that cannot disturb the mind of the wise man, none will be able to. For what? Shall fear disturb it? But fear is of those things, absent, of which, present, there is distress; distress, then, being removed, fear is removed. There remain two disturbances, exultant joy and lust; which, if they shall not befall the wise man, the mind of the wise man will always be tranquil.

Nor indeed would Atlas be said to bear up the heaven, nor Prometheus to be fastened to the Caucasus, nor starry Cepheus with his wife, his son-in-law, his daughter, unless the divine knowledge of celestial things had carried over their name to the error of fable. From these, in succession, all who placed their zeal in the contemplation of things were both held and named wise; and that name of theirs lasted down to the age of Pythagoras. Who, as Heraclides of Pontus, the hearer of Plato, a man learned among the first, writes, is said to have come to Phlius, and there to have discoursed learnedly and copiously on certain matters with Leon, chief of the Phliasians. And when Leon had admired his talent and eloquence, he asked of him in what art above all he trusted; but he said that he knew no art, but was a philosopher. Leon, wondering at the novelty of the name, asked who these philosophers were, and what difference there was between them and the rest;

— To those who are dead, or to those who must die? — To both. — It is wretched, then, since it is an evil. — Certainly. — Therefore both those to whom it has already fallen to die, and those to whom it will fall, are wretched. — So it seems to me. — Then no one is not wretched. — No one at all. — And indeed, if you wish to be consistent, all who have been born or ever shall be are not only wretched, but everlastingly wretched. For if you called only those wretched who must die, you would except no one of the living — since all must die — yet there would be an end of misery in death. But since the dead too are wretched, we are born into everlasting misery. For those who perished a hundred thousand years ago must needs be wretched — or rather, all, whoever have been born. — So in truth I judge. — Tell me, I pray:

And so the practice of the Peripatetics and the Academy, of disputing on every matter for both sides, has always pleased me — not only for this reason, that in no other way can what is likely to the truth in any matter be discovered, but also because it is the greatest exercise in speaking. Aristotle first employed it, and then those who came after him. In our own memory Philo, whom I often heard, made it his rule to deliver at one time the precepts of the rhetoricians, at another those of the philosophers; and to this practice I was brought by my friends at Tusculum, and there I spent what time was given me. And so, after we had given the forenoon to oratory, as we had done the day before, in the afternoon we went down into the Academy. The disputation there held I set forth not as one narrating it, but in nearly the same words in which it was acted and disputed. As we walked, then, this conversation was begun by us in this manner, and started from some such opening as this:

(But all disturbances of the mind the philosophers call diseases, and deny that any fool is free of these diseases. And those who are in disease are not sound; and the minds of all the foolish are in disease: therefore all the foolish are insane.) For they held that the soundness of minds lay in a certain tranquillity and steadfastness; a mind void of these things they called insanity, because in a disturbed mind, as in a body, soundness cannot exist.

So precisely I understand. — Which, then, do you prefer? That we forthwith make sail, or that, like men going out from harbour, we row a little? — What is that? For I do not understand. — Because Chrysippus and the Stoics, when they dispute about the disturbances of the mind, are for the most part occupied in dividing and defining these; very scanty is that discourse of theirs by which they would heal minds and not suffer them to be turbulent; the Peripatetics, on the other hand, bring forward much for the calming of minds, and pass over the thorns of dividing and defining. I was asking, then, whether I should spread the sails of discourse at once, or first propel it a little with the oars of the dialecticians. — That way, indeed; for the whole of what I seek will be more complete from both. — That is the more correct course;

and Pythagoras answered that the life of men seemed to him like that fair held with the greatest pomp of games, in the gathering of all Greece; for as there some sought the glory and renown of the crown by exercised bodies, others were led by the gain and profit of buying or selling, but there was a certain kind of men, and that the most freeborn, who sought neither applause nor gain, but came for the sake of looking on, and carefully observed what was done and in what manner — so we, as if from some city to the gathering of a fair, set out from another life and nature into this life: some are slaves to glory, others to money; rare are certain ones who, counting all else as nothing, zealously gaze upon the nature of things. These, he said, he called lovers of wisdom — that is, philosophers; and as there it was most freeborn to look on, acquiring nothing for oneself, so in life the contemplation and knowledge of things far surpasses all other pursuits.

do those things terrify you — the three-headed Cerberus among the dead, the roaring of Cocytus, the ferrying across Acheron, Tantalus touching the surface of the water with his chin yet wasted with thirst; then that stone which Sisyphus rolls, sweating in his straining and getting not a whit forward? For who could not, in a case of that kind? Or what difficulty is there in refuting these monstrous fancies of poets and painters?

I cannot say how greatly I was delighted, or rather aided, by your disputation of yesterday. For although I am conscious that I was never overly fond of life, yet now and then a certain fear and grief was cast before my mind, when I reflected that there would one day be an end of this light and a loss of all the goods of life. From this kind of trouble I have been so freed, believe me, that I think nothing less to be cared for. — That is no wonder at all;

And no less acutely did they name the affection of mind that lacks the light of reason amentia (\"mindlessness\") and dementia. From which it is to be understood that those who set these names upon things felt this same thing which the Stoics, having received it from Socrates, carefully retained — that all the foolish are unsound. For the mind that is in any disease — and these disturbed motions, as I just said, the philosophers call diseases — is no more sound than is a body that is in disease. So it comes about that wisdom is the soundness of the mind, but folly a kind of unsoundness, which is insanity and the same as dementia; and these things are much better marked by Latin words than by Greek.

but you shall ask afterward, if anything be somewhat obscure. — I will indeed; yet you, as you are wont, will say those very obscure things more plainly than they are said by the Greeks. — I shall strive, indeed; but there is need of an attentive mind, lest everything slip away, if some one thing escape. — Since the things which the Greeks call pathē we prefer to call disturbances rather than diseases, in explaining these I shall follow that old division — first of Pythagoras, then of Plato — who divide the mind into two parts: the one they make a partaker of reason, the other devoid of it; in the part that partakes of reason they place tranquillity, that is, a placid and quiet steadfastness, in that other the turbid motions both of anger and of desire, contrary and hostile to reason.

Nor indeed was Pythagoras only the inventor of the name, but also the amplifier of the things themselves. Who, when after this conversation at Phlius he had come into Italy, adorned that Greece which was called Magna, both privately and publicly, with most excellent institutions and arts. Of whose teaching there will perhaps be another time for speaking. But from the ancient philosophy down to Socrates, who had heard Archelaus, the disciple of Anaxagoras, numbers and motions were treated, and whence all things arose and whither they fell back, and the magnitudes, intervals, and courses of the stars were zealously inquired into by them, and all celestial things. But Socrates first called philosophy down from heaven, and set it in the cities, and even brought it into men's homes, and compelled it to inquire about life and morals and things good and evil.

— And yet there are books full of philosophers disputing against these very things. — Foolishly enough. For who is so witless as to be moved by them? — If, then, men are not wretched in the world below, neither are there any at all in the world below. — So in truth I judge. — Where, then, are those whom you call wretched, or what place do they inhabit? For if they exist, they cannot be nowhere. — For my part I think they are nowhere. — Therefore they do not even exist? — Just so; and yet wretched for this very reason, that they are nothing.

for this is what philosophy effects: it heals minds, it strips away empty anxieties, it sets us free from desires, it drives out fears. But this power of hers does not avail alike with all; she avails much when she has laid hold of a nature suited to her. For not only does fortune favour the brave, as the old proverb has it, but much more does reason, which by certain precepts, as it were, confirms the strength of fortitude. You, plainly, Nature begot lofty and high-minded and despising of human things; and so my discourse against death, addressed to a brave mind, easily found lodging. But do you think this same discourse avails with those very men, save a very few, by whom such things have been discovered, disputed, and written down? For how rare a philosopher is found so disposed in character, so established in mind and in life, as reason demands — one who counts his teaching not a parade of knowledge, but a law of living; who himself obeys himself, and submits to his own decrees?

Which will be found in many other places too; but that another time — now, what presses. The very force of the word, then, declares the whole of what we are inquiring after, what it is and of what kind. For since those must be understood to be sound whose mind is disturbed by no motion, as it were by a disease, those who are otherwise affected must of necessity be called insane. And so nothing is better than what is in the common usage of Latin speech, when we say that those have \"gone out of their power\" who are carried away unbridled either by lust or by anger — although anger itself is a part of lust; for it is thus defined: anger is the lust of avenging — those, then, who are said to have gone out of their power, are so said because they are not in the power of the mind, to which the rule of the whole soul has been assigned by Nature. But whence the Greeks call it mania I could not easily say; that very thing, however, we distinguish better than they. For this insanity, which, joined with folly, extends more widely, we separate from raving fury. The Greeks wish to, indeed, but lack the word: what we call furor they call melancholia — as though, forsooth, the mind were moved by black bile alone, and not often by anger too, when graver, or by fear or by grief; in which sense we say that Athamas, Alcmaeon, Ajax, Orestes raved. He who is so affected the Twelve Tables forbid to be master of his own affairs; and so it is written, not \"if he be insane,\" but \"if he be raving.\" For they held that folly, lacking steadfastness, that is, soundness, could nevertheless preserve a middling discharge of duties and the common and customary conduct of life; but fury they reckoned to be a blindness of the mind to all things. Which, though it seem greater than insanity, is yet of such a kind that fury can befall the wise man, but insanity cannot. But this is another question; let us return to our subject.

Let this, then, be the source; yet in describing these disturbances let us use the definitions and divisions of the Stoics, who seem to me to handle this question most acutely. This, then, is the definition of Zeno: that a disturbance — what he calls pathos — is a commotion of the mind turned away from right reason and contrary to nature. Some more briefly say that a disturbance is a too-vehement craving; but they would have that craving to be too vehement which has departed further from the constancy of nature. The parts of disturbances they hold to be born from two imagined goods and from two imagined evils; so that there are four: from goods, lust and joy — joy being of present goods, lust of future ones; from evils, they think fear and distress are born — fear from things to come, distress from things present; for the things which, coming, are feared, these same, being at hand, affect with distress.

Whose manifold method of disputing, and variety of matters, and greatness of talent, consecrated by the memory and the writings of Plato, produced several kinds of dissenting philosophers; of whom we have followed that one above all which we thought Socrates used — to conceal our own opinion, to relieve others of error, and in every disputation to seek what was most like the truth. Which custom, since Carneades held it most acutely and most copiously, we did both often at other times, and lately at Tusculum, that we should dispute after that manner. And the conversation of four days we have written out and sent to you in the former books; but on the fifth day, when we had sat down in the same place, this was proposed, on which we should dispute:

— By now I would rather you feared Cerberus than spoke things so ill-considered. — How so, pray? — The same one whom you deny to exist, you say exists. Where is that sharpness of yours? For when you say he is wretched, you say that one who does not exist exists. — I am not so dull as to say that. — What, then, do you say? — That, for example's sake, Marcus Crassus is wretched, who lost that great fortune by his death; that Gnaeus Pompeius is wretched, who was bereft of so great a glory; in short, that all are wretched who are deprived of this light of day. — You roll back to the same place. For they must exist, if they are wretched; but you were just now denying that those exist who are dead. If, then, they do not exist, they can be nothing; and so they are not even wretched. — Perhaps I am not saying even what I feel; for that very thing — not to exist, when one has existed — I count most wretched. — What?

One may see some men of such levity and ostentation that it had been better for them not to have learned at all; others greedy of money, some of glory, many the slaves of their lusts — so that their lives are wondrously at war with their words. And this seems to me most disgraceful of all. For just as, if a man professing to be a grammarian should speak barbarously, or if one who would be held a musician should sing out of tune, he is the more disgraced because he errs in the very thing whose knowledge he professes, so a philosopher who errs in the conduct of life is the more disgraced because he stumbles in the duty whose master he would be, and, having professed the art of living, transgresses in his living. — Is it not then to be feared, if it is as you say, that you adorn philosophy with a false glory? For what greater proof is there that it profits nothing, than that certain finished philosophers live disgracefully?

You said, I think, that distress seemed to you to befall the wise man. — And indeed so I judge. — Human that, that you so judge. For we were not born of flint, but there is naturally in our minds something tender and soft, which is shaken by distress as by a storm. And not absurdly did Crantor — who was among the very foremost noble men in our Academy — say: \"I by no means assent to those who so greatly praise that I-know-not-what insensibility, which neither can nor ought to be. Let me not be sick; but if I am, let feeling be present, whether something be cut or torn from the body. For that feeling no pain comes not without a great price of inhumanity in the mind, of stupor in the body.\"

Joy, however, and lust are concerned with an opinion of goods, since lust is enticed and inflamed and snatched toward that which seems good, while joy is carried away and exults at having now attained something desired. For all by nature follow those things which seem goods, and flee their contraries; wherefore, as soon as the appearance of anything is presented which seems good, nature itself impels toward attaining it. When this is done steadily and prudently, the Stoics call such craving boulēsis; let us call it will (voluntas); they think it is in the wise man alone; which they thus define: will is that which desires something with reason. But that which is roused too vehemently, reason opposing, is lust or unbridled desire, which is found in all the foolish.

It does not seem to me that virtue can be sufficient for living happily. — But, by Hercules, to my Brutus it seems so, whose judgement I — by your leave I would say it — far prefer to yours. — I do not doubt — nor is that now the matter — how much you love him, but this, of what sort that is which I have said seems so to me, on which I wish to be disputed by you. — You deny, then, that virtue can be sufficient for living happily? — I deny it entirely. — What? Toward living rightly, honourably, praiseworthily — in fine, toward living well — is there enough protection in virtue? — Surely enough. — Can you, then, either not call wretched the man who lives badly, or deny that he whom you confess to live well lives happily? — Why should I not be able? For even amid torments one can live rightly, honourably, praiseworthily, and for that reason well — provided you understand what I now call \"well.\" For I mean steadfastly, gravely, wisely, bravely.

more wretched than never to have existed at all? Then those who are not yet born are already wretched, because they do not exist; and we, if after death we are to be wretched, were wretched before we were born. But I do not remember being wretched before I was born; and if your memory is better, I should like to know whether you recall anything of yourself. — You jest, as though I said that those are wretched who have not been born, and not rather that those are wretched who are dead. — You say, then, that they exist. — No, but that, because they do not exist, having once existed, they are for that reason wretched. — Do you not see that you speak self-contradiction? For what is more contradictory than that one who does not exist should be not merely wretched, but anything at all? When you go out by the Capene Gate and see the tombs of the Calatini, the Scipios, the Servilii, the Metelli, do you think those men wretched? — Since you press me on a word, hereafter I shall not say that they "are" wretched, but only "wretched," for this very reason, that they do not exist. — You do not say, then, "Marcus Crassus is wretched," but only "wretched Marcus Crassus"? — Precisely. — As though whatever you assert in that fashion must not be either true or false! Are you not even versed in logic?

That, indeed, is no proof at all. For as not all fields that are tilled are fruitful — and false is that saying of Accius: \"Though seeds of good be sown in poorer soil, / Yet they by their own nature shine forth still\" — so not all minds that are cultivated bear fruit. And, to dwell on the same comparison: as a field, however fertile, cannot be fruitful without cultivation, so neither can a mind without instruction; each thing without the other is feeble. But the cultivation of the mind is philosophy; this plucks out vices by the roots and prepares minds to receive sowing, and commits to them and, so to speak, sows what, when grown, may bear the richest fruits. Let us proceed, then, as we have begun. Say, if you please, on what you wish the disputation to turn. —

But let us see whether this be the language of men who flatter our weakness and indulge our softness; let us rather dare not only to lop off the branches of miseries, but to pluck out all the fibres of the roots. Yet something perhaps will be left — so deep are the roots of folly; but only that will be left which shall be necessary. This, indeed, hold for certain: unless the mind be healed — which cannot come about without philosophy — there will be no end of miseries. Wherefore, since we have begun, let us hand ourselves over to philosophy to be cured: we shall be healed, if we are willing. And I will go even further: for I shall treat not of distress alone — though that indeed first — but of every disturbance, as I have put it, of the mind, every disease, as the Greeks will have it. And first, if you please, let us proceed in the manner of the Stoics, who are wont to bind up their arguments briefly; then we shall range after our own fashion.

And likewise, when we are so moved that we are in some good, this happens in two ways. For when the mind is moved placidly and steadily with reason, then that is called gladness (gaudium); but when the mind exults emptily and extravagantly, then that may be called exultant or excessive joy, which they thus define: an elation of the mind without reason. And since, as by nature we crave goods, so by nature we turn away from evils, that turning-away, when it shall be done with reason, let it be called caution (cautio), and let it be understood to be in the wise man alone; but that which is without reason and with a low and broken faint-heartedness, let it be named fear: fear, then, is a caution turned away from reason.

These things are thrown even on the rack, to which the happy life does not aspire. — What, then? Is the happy life alone, I ask, left outside the door and threshold of the prison, when steadfastness, gravity, fortitude, wisdom, and the rest of the virtues are dragged to the torturer and refuse neither punishment nor pain? — You, if you mean to do anything, must seek out something new; those things move me least of all, not only because they are commonplace, but much more because, just as certain light wines have no force in water, so those sayings of the Stoics delight when tasted rather than when drunk. As that chorus of virtues, set upon the rack, places images before the eyes with the most ample dignity, so that the happy life seems about to go swiftly toward them and not to suffer them to be deserted by it;

For first of all this is laid down: that every proposition (for so it occurs to me for the present to render axioma; I shall use another term later if I find a better) — this, then, is a proposition, which is either true or false. When, therefore, you say "wretched Marcus Crassus," either you say "Crassus is wretched," so that it may be judged whether it be true or false, or you say nothing at all. — Come, I now grant that those who are dead are not wretched, since you have wrung from me the admission that those who do not exist at all cannot even be wretched. But what of this? We who live, since we must die, are we not wretched? For what sweetness can there be in life, when day and night one must reflect that at any moment one must die? — And do you grasp how great an evil you have cast off from the human condition?

I hold pain to be the greatest of all evils. — Even greater than disgrace? — That, for my part, I do not dare to say; and I am ashamed to have been so quickly thrown from my opinion. — You would have more cause for shame, were you to persist in it. For what is less worthy than that anything should seem to you worse than dishonour, infamy, baseness? To escape these, what pain is not only not to be refused, but to be sought of one's own accord, taken upon oneself, welcomed? — So indeed I judge. Therefore, granted that pain be not the highest evil, an evil it certainly is. — Do you see, then, how much, on a brief admonition, you have abated of the terror of pain?

He who is brave is also confident (since confidens, by a bad habit of speaking, is reckoned a fault, though the word is drawn from confiding, which is a thing of praise). But he who is confident certainly does not fear; for to confide is at variance with fearing. Now, into whomsoever distress falls, into the same falls fear; for those things by whose presence we are in distress, the same, impending and coming, we fear. So it comes about that distress is at war with fortitude. It is likely, then, that into whomsoever distress falls, into the same fall both fear and a breaking, indeed, of the mind and a casting down. And into whomsoever these fall, into the same it falls to be a slave, and, if ever, to confess himself conquered. And he who admits these must needs admit also timidity and cowardice. But these do not befall the brave man: therefore neither does distress. But no one is wise unless brave: distress, then, will not befall the wise man.

But of a present evil there is no affection in the wise man; that of the foolish is distress, and by it they are affected in imagined evils, and they let down and contract their minds, not obeying reason. And so this is the first definition: that distress is a contraction of the mind, reason opposing. Thus there are four disturbances, three steadfast states (constantiae), since to distress no steadfast state is opposed. But they think all disturbances come about by judgement and opinion. And so they define them more precisely, that it may be understood not only how vicious they are, but also how much they are in our power. Distress, then, is a fresh opinion of a present evil, in which it seems right that the mind be let down and contracted; joy, a fresh opinion of a present good, in which it seems right to be carried away; fear, an opinion of an impending evil which seems intolerable; lust, an opinion of a coming good, which would be advantageous if it were already present and at hand.

but when you have led the mind away from that picture and those images of the virtues to the fact and the truth, this is left bare — whether anyone can be happy as long as he is tortured. Wherefore let us now inquire into this; but do not fear that the virtues will protest and complain that they have been left behind by the happy life. For if no virtue is free of prudence, prudence herself sees this — that not all the good are also happy; and she recalls many things about Marcus Atilius, Quintus Caepio, Manius Aquilius, and prudence herself holds back the happy life, when it tries to go upon the rack — if you prefer to use images rather than the things themselves — and denies that it has anything in common with pain and torment.

— In what way? — Because, if death were wretched even for the dead, we should have in life a kind of infinite and everlasting evil; but now I see the goal-line, and when the course has been run to it, there is nothing further to be dreaded. But you seem to me to follow the opinion of Epicharmus, a man as shrewd as he was not without wit, Sicilian that he was. — What opinion? For I do not know it. — I shall tell it, if I can, in Latin; for you know that I am no more wont to speak Greek in a Latin discourse than Latin in a Greek one. — And rightly so. But what, pray, is that opinion of Epicharmus? — "I do not wish to die, but to be dead I count as nothing." — Now I recognize the Greek. But since you have compelled me to grant that those who are dead are not wretched, complete the work, if you can, so that I may not think it wretched even to have to die.

I see it plainly; but I want more. — I shall make the attempt; but it is a great matter, and I have need of a mind that does not resist. — That you shall have; for as I did yesterday, so now I shall follow reason wherever it leads me. — First, then, I shall speak of the weakness of many men, and of the various schools of the philosophers. Their chief, both in authority and in antiquity, the Socratic Aristippus, did not hesitate to call pain the highest evil. Then to this nerveless and womanish opinion Epicurus showed himself pupil enough. After him Hieronymus of Rhodes said that to be free of pain was the highest good: so great an evil did he reckon in pain. The rest — save Zeno, Aristo, Pyrrho — say much what you just now said: an evil indeed, but others are worse.

Besides, it is necessary that he who is brave be also of great soul; he who is of great soul, unconquered; he who is unconquered, that he despise human things and reckon them set beneath him. But no one can despise those things on account of which he can be affected with distress; from which it follows that the brave man is never affected with distress. But all the wise are brave: therefore distress does not befall the wise man. And just as an eye that is disturbed is not rightly disposed for performing its function, and as the remaining parts, or the whole body, when it is moved from its proper state, fail of their office and function, so a disturbed mind is not fit to discharge its office. But the office of the mind is to use reason well; and the mind of the wise man is always so disposed that it uses reason most excellently; therefore it is never disturbed. But distress is a disturbance of the mind: therefore the wise man will always be free of it.

But the judgements and the opinions which I have said the disturbances to be — not in these alone do they say the disturbances are placed, but those things too which are effected by the disturbances: as that distress effects a kind of bite, as it were, of pain; fear, a certain recoiling and flight of the mind; joy, an effusive cheerfulness; lust, an unbridled craving. And opinion (opinatio), which we have included in all the foregoing definitions, they hold to be a weak assent.

I readily allow you to proceed in that fashion, although it is unjust for you to prescribe to me in what manner you wish me to dispute. But I ask whether we think that anything was accomplished on the former days, or nothing. — Accomplished, indeed, and a good deal. — And yet, if it is so, this question is now half-finished and almost brought to its end. — In what manner, pray? — Because turbulent motions and tossings of minds, roused and carried away by inconsiderate impulse, repelling all reason, leave no part of the happy life. For who, fearing death or pain — of which the one is often present, the other ever impends — can be not wretched? What if the same man, as generally happens, fears poverty, ignominy, infamy, if weakness, blindness, if, finally — what has often befallen not single men but powerful peoples — slavery?

— That indeed is no trouble at all, but I am attempting greater things. — How is this no trouble? Or what, pray, are those greater things? — Because, since after death there is no evil, not even death is an evil, the time next to which is after death, in which you grant there is no evil: so it is not an evil even to have to die; for that is to arrive at that which we confess to be no evil. — Unfold this more fully, I pray. For these points, being rather thorny, compel me to confess before I assent. But what are those greater things which you say you are attempting? — To show, if I can, that death is not only not an evil, but even a good. — That, indeed, I do not demand; yet I long to hear it. For even if you do not achieve what you wish, still you will achieve this, that death is not an evil. But I shall not interrupt you at all; I would rather hear a continuous discourse. — What if I should ask you something?

Therefore that which Nature herself, and a certain noble virtue, straightway rejects — namely, that you should call pain the highest evil, and be driven from the opinion by setting disgrace against it — in this philosophy, the teacher of life, persists for so many ages. What duty, what praise, what honour will be worth so much that the man who has persuaded himself that pain is the highest evil would wish to attain it at the cost of bodily pain? What disgrace, what baseness, on the other hand, will a man not endure, to escape pain, if he has decided that pain is the highest evil? And who is not wretched — not only then, when he is pressed by the utmost pains, if in these lies the highest evil, but even when he knows that this can befall him? And who is there to whom it cannot befall? So it comes about that absolutely no one can be happy.

This, too, is likely: that he who is temperate — whom the Greeks call sōphrōn, and that virtue sōphrosynē, which I am wont to call now temperance, now moderation, sometimes even modesty; but I am not sure whether that virtue may rightly be called frugality, which among the Greeks has a narrower meaning, who call frugi men chrēsimous, that is, merely useful; but our word is wider; for every abstinence, all harmlessness (which among the Greeks has no customary name, but can have ablabeia; for harmlessness is such an affection of mind as harms no one) — the other virtues too frugality contains. And unless it were so great, and if it were held within those narrow bounds in which most suppose, the surname of Lucius Piso would never have been so greatly praised.

But under single disturbances are placed several parts of the same kind: as under distress, envy (invidentia) — for the less customary word must be used for teaching's sake, since invidia is spoken of not only of him who envies, but also of him who is envied — emulation, disparagement, pity, anguish, mourning, grief, hardship, pain, lamentation, anxiety, trouble, affliction, despair, and any others of the same kind. Under fear are placed sluggishness, shame, terror, timidity, panic, faintness, confusion, dread; under pleasure, malevolence rejoicing at another's ill, delight, vaunting, and the like; under lust, anger, irascibility, hatred, enmity, discord, want, longing, and the rest of that kind. These they define in this manner: they say that envy is a distress taken up on account of another's prosperity, which does no harm to the envier.

Can anyone, fearing these, be happy? What of him who not only fears these as things to come, but even bears and sustains them present — add to these too exile, mourning, bereavements: he who, broken by these things, is crushed by distress, can he at last be not most wretched? But what of that man whom we see inflamed with lusts and raging, ravenously seeking all things with insatiable desire, and the more abundantly he draws pleasures from every side, so much the more heavily and ardently thirsting — would you not rightly call him most wretched? What of that man, carried away by levity and exulting in empty joy and rashly exultant — is he not the more wretched, the happier he seems to himself? Therefore, as these men are wretched, so on the contrary those are happy whom no fears terrify, no distresses eat away, no lusts rouse, no futile exultant joys melt away with languid pleasures. As, then, the tranquillity of the sea is understood when not even the slightest breeze moves the waves, so the quiet and calm state of the mind is discerned when there is no disturbance by which it can be moved. But if there is one who counts the force of fortune, and all human things which can befall anyone, bearable, so that neither fear nor anguish touches him, and the same man, if he covets nothing, is carried away by no empty pleasure of the mind, what reason is there why he should not be happy?

will you not answer? — That would be arrogant; but, unless something makes it necessary, I would rather you did not ask. — I shall humour you, and will explain as best I can the things you wish — yet not like the Pythian Apollo, as though what I say were sure and fixed, but as one poor man among many, following what is probable by conjecture. For I have no means of advancing further than to see what is like the truth; certainties are for those who both declare that such things can be perceived and profess themselves to be wise men. — As you please; we are ready to listen.

Metrodorus, indeed, thinks that man perfectly happy whose body is well constituted, and who is assured it will ever be so. But who is the man who can have that assurance? Epicurus, in truth, says things that to me at least seem to court ridicule. For he affirms in one place that, if a wise man be burnt, if he be racked — you expect, perhaps, that he will say: he will bear it, he will endure it, he will not give in; great praise, by Hercules, and worthy of that very god by whom I have sworn. But for Epicurus, a harsh and hard man, this is not enough: \"If he be in the bull of Phalaris,\" he will say, \"how sweet this is! how I care nothing for it!\" Sweet, even? Is it not enough that it be not bitter? Why, this very thing even those who deny that pain is an evil are not wont to say — that to be racked is sweet to anyone: harsh, hard, hateful, contrary to Nature they call it, yet not an evil. But this man, who calls it the one evil and the extreme of all evils, holds that the wise man will call it sweet.

But because neither he who through fear has abandoned his post, which is cowardice, nor he who through avarice has not returned a deposit secretly given, which is injustice, nor he who through rashness has managed an affair badly, which is folly, is wont to be called frugi, therefore frugality has embraced three virtues — fortitude, justice, prudence (although this indeed is common to the virtues, for all are linked and yoked among themselves): the remaining and fourth virtue, then, would be frugality itself. For it seems to be its proper office to rule and calm the motions of a desiring mind, and, ever opposing lust, to preserve a moderate steadfastness in everything. The vice contrary to it is called worthlessness (nequitia).

(For if anyone grieve at the prosperity of one by whom he himself is hurt, he would not rightly be said to envy, as if Agamemnon at Hector; but he who, though another's advantages do him no harm, yet grieves that the other enjoys them — he, assuredly, envies.) Emulation (aemulatio), indeed, is spoken of in two ways, so that this name is both in praise and in fault; for the imitation of virtue is called emulation — but with that we have nothing to do in this place, for it is a thing of praise — and there is also emulation that is a distress, if another enjoys that which one desired, while oneself lacks it. But disparagement (obtrectatio) is that which I wish to be understood as zēlotypia, a distress arising from this — that another too enjoys that which one has oneself desired.

And if these things are effected by virtue, what reason is there why virtue itself, of itself, should not make men happy? — And yet the one cannot but be said, that those who fear nothing, are anguished by nothing, covet nothing, are carried away by no unbridled joy, are happy; and so this I grant you; but the other is no longer entire. For by the former disputations it has been effected that the wise man is free of every disturbance of the mind. — Then doubtless the matter is finished;

— First, then, we must see what death itself, which seems the most familiar of things, really is. For there are some who think death to be the departure of the soul from the body; some who think no departure takes place, but that soul and body perish together, the soul being extinguished within the body. Of those who hold that the soul departs, some think it is straightway scattered, some that it endures for a long time, some forever. As to what the soul itself is, moreover, or where, or whence, there is great disagreement. To some the heart itself seems to be the soul, whence men are called "heart-less," "wit-less," and "of one heart," and the famous Nasica, twice consul, was called Corculum, "Little Heart," and "a man of excellent heart, the shrewd Aelius Sextus." Empedocles holds the soul to be the blood suffused about the heart; to others a certain part of the brain has seemed to hold the sovereignty of the soul; to others neither the heart itself nor any part of the brain seems to be the soul,

I do not require of you that you treat pain in the same words in which Epicurus, a man, as you know, given to pleasure, treats pleasure. Let him say, by all means, the same thing in the bull of Phalaris that he would say if he were on his little couch; I do not attribute so great a power to wisdom against pain. If a man is brave in enduring it, that suffices for duty; that he should even rejoice, I do not require. For it is a grievous thing, beyond doubt — harsh, bitter, hostile to Nature, hard to suffer and to bear. Look at Philoctetes, to whom one must grant his groaning;

Frugality, as I think, is from \"fruit\" (frux), than which nothing better comes from the earth; worthlessness from this (though this perhaps will be somewhat harsh — but let us try; let us be thought to have jested, if it comes to nothing) — from the fact that there is nothing-to-any-purpose (nequicquam) in such a man, whence the same man is called \"good for nothing\" (nihili). — He, then, who is frugi, or, if you prefer, moderate and temperate, must needs be steadfast; and he who is steadfast, calm; he who is calm, free of all disturbance, therefore of distress too. And those things belong to the wise man: distress, then, will be absent from the wise man. And so not unskillfully does Dionysius of Heraclea argue against those words which Achilles in Homer complains, in this manner, I think: \"And my heart deep within swells with sorrowful angers, when I recall myself bereft of honour and of all renown.\" Is a hand rightly affected when it is in a swelling, or does any other limb whatever, when swollen and turgid, hold itself otherwise than viciously?

Pity is a distress arising from the misery of another suffering wrongfully (for no one is moved with pity at the punishment of a parricide or a traitor); anguish, an oppressing distress; mourning, a distress arising from the bitter death of one who was dear; grief, a tearful distress; hardship, a laborious distress; pain, a torturing distress; lamentation, a distress with wailing; anxiety, a distress with thought; trouble, an abiding distress; affliction, a distress with vexation of the body; despair, a distress without any expectation of better things. But those things which are placed under fear they thus define: sluggishness, a fear of toil to follow;

for the question seems to have come to its end. — Pretty nearly, indeed. — But yet that is the manner of mathematicians, not of philosophers. For geometers, when they wish to teach something, if anything of what they have taught before pertains to that matter, take it for granted and proved, and only explain that of which nothing has been written before; but philosophers, whatever matter they have in hand, heap into it all things which suit it, even if they have been disputed in another place. For unless it were so, why would a Stoic, if it were asked whether virtue could be sufficient for living happily, say much? To whom it would be enough to answer that he had taught before that nothing is good save what is honourable, this being proved, it follows that the happy life is content with virtue; and as this is consequent on that, so that on this — that, if the happy life is content with virtue, then nothing is good save what is honourable.

but some have said the seat and place of the soul is in the heart, others in the brain. The soul, moreover, some call anima, the breath — as most of our people do; and the name declares it: for we say "to draw breath" (agere animam) and "to breathe out" (efflare), and call men "spirited" (animosi) and "well-disposed" (bene animati) and speak of acting "from the heart's intent" (ex animi sententia); the soul itself (animus) is named from breath (anima). To Zeno the Stoic the soul seems to be fire. But these things I have named — heart, brain, breath, fire — the common run hold; the rest, mostly, single thinkers hold. As, long before, the ancients, and most recently Aristoxenus, a musician and likewise a philosopher, held the soul to be a certain tension of the body itself, like the thing called harmony in song and on the strings: so that out of the nature and figure of the whole body various motions are stirred up, as sounds are in song.

for he had seen Hercules himself upon Oeta crying out at the greatness of his pains. Nothing, then, consoled this man, not even the arrows he had received from Hercules, when \"the veins of his inward parts, steeped with venom from the viper's bite, stir up foul torments.\" And so he cries out, seeking aid, longing to die: \"Alas, who will commit me to the briny waves / From the high summit of the cliff! / Now, now I waste away; the force of the wound, / The fire of the ulcer, consumes my soul.\" It seems hard to say that a man is not in evil — and in great evil too — who is forced so to cry out.

So, then, an inflated and swelling mind is in vice. But the mind of the wise man is always free of vice, never swells, never grows turgid; but the mind of an angry man is of this kind: therefore the wise man is never angry. For if he is angry, he also desires; for it is proper to an angry man to desire to brand with the greatest possible pain him by whom he seems to have been hurt. And he who has desired this must needs, if he has attained it, greatly rejoice. From which it comes about that he rejoices at another's ill; which, since it does not befall the wise man, neither does it befall him to be angry. But if distress befell the wise man, anger too would befall him; and since he is free of that, he will be free of distress also.

...terror, a fear that shakes, from which it comes about that a blush follows shame, paleness and trembling and chattering of teeth follow terror; timidity, a fear of an approaching evil; panic, a fear moving the mind from its place, whence that line of Ennius: \"then panic drives all wisdom from my breast, made lifeless\"; faintness, a fear following and as it were the companion of panic; confusion, a fear shaking out one's thoughts; dread, an abiding fear.

But yet they do not so proceed; for there are separate books both on the honourable and on the highest good, and although from this it is effected that there is a great enough force in virtue toward living happily, nonetheless they treat this separately. For each matter must be handled with its own proper arguments and admonitions, especially one so great. For beware lest you think that any voice more glorious was ever uttered in philosophy, or that there is any promise of philosophy richer or greater. For what does she profess? O good gods! That she will bring it about that he who has obeyed her laws shall be ever armed against fortune, shall have all the protections of living well and happily in himself — in fine, shall be ever happy.

He did not stray from his own craft, and yet he said something which, whatever its worth, had been said and explained long before by Plato. Xenocrates denied that the soul has any shape or, as it were, body, and said it is number, whose power, as had already been Pythagoras's view, is greatest in nature. His teacher Plato fashioned a threefold soul, whose sovereign part — that is, reason — he placed in the head as in a citadel; and the two other parts he willed to obey, namely anger and desire, which he separated into their own places: anger in the breast, desire he set beneath the midriff.

But let us look at Hercules himself, who was broken by pain at the very time when by death itself he was seeking immortality. What words does he utter in Sophocles, in the Trachiniae!
