When Deianira had put upon him the tunic dyed with the Centaur's blood, and it had cleaved to his flesh, he says: \"O things grievous to tell, harsh to endure, / Which, drained out, I have borne in body and in soul! / Neither did Juno's relentless terror, / Nor sullen Eurystheus, bring me so much ill / As one frenzied woman, the child of Oeneus' birth. / She has snared me unawares in a robe of madness, / Which, clinging to my sides, rends my flesh with its bite / And, pressing hard, draws off the breath of my lungs: / Already it has sucked up all my discoloured blood. / Thus my body, consumed by horrible ruin, has wasted away; / I myself, fast bound, am slain by a woven plague. / This neither an enemy's hand, nor the Earth-born / Mass of the Giants, nor the Centaur with his double-formed onset / Inflicted upon my body, / No power of Greece, no barbarian savagery, / No fierce race banished to the ends of the earth, / Through all of which, ranging, I drove out every wildness — / But I, a man, am slain by a woman, by a woman's hand. / O son, lay true claim to this name for your father, / Let not a mother's love prevail over my death. / Snatch her hither to me, torn from those dutiful hands; / Now shall I see whether you hold her or me the dearer.

For indeed, if the wise man could fall into distress, he could fall also into pity, could fall into envy (I did not say invidia, which is when one is envied; but from \"envying\" (invidere) invidentia can rightly be formed, that we may escape the ambiguous word invidia). Which word is drawn from \"gazing too much\" (nimis intueri) at another's fortune, as it is in the Melanippus: \"Who, then, has envied (invidit) the flower of my children?\" It seems bad Latin, but Accius spoke admirably; for, as we say videre florem (\"to see the flower\"), so to say invidere florem is more correct than invidere flori. We are forbidden by usage;

The parts of pleasure they describe in this manner: that malevolence is a pleasure from another's ill without one's own profit; delight, a pleasure soothing the mind by the sweetness of hearing; and such as this is, of the ears, such are those of the eyes and of touches and of smells and of tastes, which are all of one kind, pleasures, as it were, liquefied for drenching the mind. Vaunting (iactatio) is a pleasure exultant and carrying itself too insolently.

But I shall see what she effects; meanwhile this very thing I greatly esteem, that she promises it. For Xerxes, indeed, stuffed with all the prizes and gifts of fortune, content with neither cavalry, nor foot-forces, nor multitude of ships, nor boundless weight of gold, set a prize for him who should discover a new pleasure — with which itself he was not content; for lust will never find an end — I should wish that we could elicit by a prize one who would bring us something whereby we might more firmly believe this.

Dicaearchus, however, in that discourse which he reports as held at Corinth in three books, makes many learned men dispute in the first book; in the two others he brings on a certain aged Pherecrates of Phthia, whom he says was sprung from Deucalion, arguing that there is no soul at all, and that this name is wholly empty, and that it is in vain that we call things "living" and "animate," since there is no soul or breath within man or within beast; and that all the power by which we either act or feel is spread equally throughout all living bodies and is not separable from the body, being indeed nothing, nor is there anything except a single and simple body, so fashioned that by the tempering of its nature it has life and feeling.

Go on, dare, my son! weep over your father's torments, / Have pity: nations shall bewail our miseries. / Alas, that I should send forth a maiden's wailing from my mouth, / I whom no one ever saw groaning at any ill! / Effeminate, my virtue, struck down, perishes. / Come near, my son, stand by, look upon the piteous / Disembowelled body of your mangled father! / Behold, all of you, and you, Father of the heavenly ones, / Hurl, I beseech, upon me the flashing force of your thunderbolt! / Now, now the anguished crests of my pains torment me, / Now creeps the burning. O hands once victorious,

the poet kept his own right and spoke more boldly. — Into the same man, then, falls both to pity and to envy. For he who grieves at another's adversities grieves also at another's prosperities, as Theophrastus, deploring the death of his companion Callisthenes, is vexed at the prosperous affairs of Alexander, and so says that Callisthenes fell in with a man of the highest power and the highest fortune, but ignorant of how it befitted him to use prosperity. Now, as pity is a distress arising from another's adversities, so envy is a distress arising from another's prosperities. Into whomsoever, then, pity falls, into the same falls also envy; but envy does not befall the wise man: therefore neither does pity. But if the wise man were wont to take things ill, he would be wont also to pity. Distress, then, is absent from the wise man.

But the things placed under lust are thus defined: that anger is a lust of punishing him who seems to have hurt one by injury; irascibility (excandescentia), an anger arising and just now existing, which in Greek is called thymōsis; hatred, an inveterate anger; enmity, an anger watching for a time of avenging; discord, a sharper anger conceived in the inmost mind and heart; want, an insatiable lust; longing, a lust of seeing one who is not yet present. They also distinguish this — that lust is of those things which are spoken of some one or some several things, which the dialecticians call katēgorēmata (predicates), as to have riches, to take offices; but want is of the things themselves, as of offices, of money.

I should wish that indeed, but I have a little something to ask. For I assent that of the things you have laid down the one is consequent on the other, so that, as, if what is honourable be alone good, it follows that the happy life is made complete by virtue, so, if the happy life be in virtue, that nothing is good save virtue. But your Brutus, on the authority of Aristo and Antiochus, does not think this; for he thinks that there is some good besides virtue. — What then?

Aristotle — far excelling all others, save that I always except Plato, both in genius and in diligence — when he had embraced those four familiar kinds of first principles from which all things arise, holds that there is a certain fifth nature, from which mind comes. For to think, to foresee, to learn, to teach, to discover something, to remember so many things, to love and to hate, to desire and to fear, to be troubled and to rejoice — these things and the like, he holds, are in none of those four kinds; he brings in a fifth kind, lacking a name, and so he calls the soul itself by a new name, endelecheia, as it were a certain continuous and perpetual motion. Unless perhaps some escape me, these are nearly all the opinions about the soul. For Democritus — a great man indeed, but one who makes the soul out of smooth and round little bodies by a kind of chance concourse — let us pass him over; for there is nothing among those men which the swarm of atoms does not bring to pass.

O breasts, O back, O muscled brawn of my arms, / Was it by your crushing that once the Nemean lion, / Gnashing, breathed out heavily his last breath? / Did this right hand, with the foul she-serpent slain, / Pacify Lerna? Did this lay low the two-bodied band? / Did this cast down the Erymanthian, the ravaging beast? / Did this draw up from the dark Tartarean region / The three-headed dog, born of the Hydra's brood? / Did this slay, with its manifold coils, / The dragon that guarded with watchful eye the gold-bearing tree? / Many other things has our victorious hand visited, / Nor did anyone take spoils from our glories.\" Can we, then, despise pain, when we see Hercules himself grieving so beyond endurance?

These things are thus stated by the Stoics and concluded somewhat too crookedly. But they must sometimes be stated more amply and at greater length; yet one must use above all the opinions of those who employ the most courageous and, so to speak, manly reasoning and sentiment. For the Peripatetics, our friends, than whom nothing is richer, nothing more learned, nothing weightier, do not at all win my approval with their middling allowances of disturbances or diseases of the mind. For every evil, even a middling one, is an evil; but we are aiming at this — that there be none at all in the wise man. For as a body, even if it is moderately sick, is not sound, so in the mind this middling state lacks soundness. And so our countrymen, admirably, as in many other matters, named trouble, anxiety, anguish aegritudo (\"sickness\" of mind, distress), from the likeness of sick bodies.

They say that the fount of all disturbances is intemperance, which is a falling away of the whole mind from right reason, so turned away from the prescription of reason that in no way can the cravings of the mind either be ruled or be restrained. As, then, temperance calms the cravings and brings it about that they obey right reason, and preserves the considered judgements of the mind, so intemperance, hostile to it, inflames, confounds, rouses the whole state of the mind; and so both distresses and fears and all the remaining disturbances are begotten from it. As, when the blood is corrupted, or when phlegm or bile overflows, diseases and sicknesses arise in the body, so the confusion of depraved opinions, and their mutual repugnance, strips the mind of soundness and disturbs it with diseases;

Do you think I shall speak against Brutus? — Why, as it seems; for to set bounds beforehand is not mine. — What, then, is consistent for each, in another place. For that disagreement was mine both with Antiochus often, and with Aristo lately, when, as commander, I lodged at his house in Athens. For it did not seem to me that anyone could be happy while in evils; but that the wise man could be in evils, if there were any evils of body or of fortune. These things were said — which Antiochus too wrote in several places — that virtue itself, of itself, could make the happy life, but yet not the happiest; then that most things are named from the greater part, even if some part be absent, as strength, as health, as riches, as office, as glory, which are discerned by kind, not by number; likewise that the happy life, even if in some part it limped, yet from a much greater part keeps its own name.

Which of these opinions is true, some god may see; which is likest the truth is a great question. Do we, then, prefer to decide among these opinions, or to return to our proposed theme? — I should wish both, if it could be; but it is hard to mingle them. Wherefore, if without discussing those matters we can be freed from the fear of death, let us do that; but if that cannot be done save by unfolding this question of the soul, let us take this now, if you think fit, and the other another time. — What I perceive you prefer, that I think the more convenient; for reasoning will bring it about that, whichever of the opinions I have set forth be true, death is either no evil or rather a good.

Let Aeschylus come forward, who was not a poet only, but a Pythagorean too — for so we have been told. How, in him, does Prometheus bear the pain which he undergoes for the theft from Lemnos — \"whence fire is famed to have been secretly parcelled out to mortals; the cunning Prometheus stole it by guile, and paid the penalties to Jove by supreme decree\"? Paying these penalties, then, fastened to the Caucasus, he says this: \"Offspring of the Titans, sharers of our blood, / Begotten of Heaven, behold me bound to the rugged / And fettering rocks, as on a roaring strait / Timid sailors, fearing the night, make fast their ship. / Thus has Saturnian Jupiter fixed me, / And the will of Jove enlisted the hands of Mulciber. / These wedges, driving them in by cruel craft, / He drove through my limbs; whereby, wretched, by such skill / Transfixed, I dwell in this fortress of the Furies.

By a word nearly the same the Greeks call every disturbance of the mind; for they call pathos, that is, disease, whatever turbid motion there is in the mind. We do better: for distress is most like sick bodies; but lust is not like sickness, nor is immoderate joy, which is a pleasure of the mind elated and exultant. Even fear itself is not very like disease, although it is the neighbour of distress; but properly, as \"sickness\" (aegrotatio) in the body, so \"distress\" (aegritudo) in the mind has a name not severed from pain. The origin of this pain, then, must be unfolded by us — that is, the cause that effects distress in the mind as sickness in the body. For as physicians, when the cause of a disease is found, think the cure found, so we, when the cause of distress is discovered, shall discover the means of healing.

but from the disturbances are made, first, diseases, which they call nosēmata, and those things which are contrary to those diseases, which have a vicious aversion and loathing toward fixed objects; then sicknesses, which are called by the Stoics arrōstēmata, and likewise the aversions opposed and contrary to these. In this place too much labour is spent by the Stoics, especially by Chrysippus, while the likeness of the diseases of the mind is compared to the diseases of the body; which discourse being passed over as least necessary, let us handle those things which contain the matter.

These things it is not now so necessary to pick out, although they do not seem to me said most consistently. For both, in the case of one who is happy, I do not understand what he should want, that he be happier — for if there is anything lacking, he is not even happy — and as for their saying that each thing is named and regarded from the greater part, there are cases where that holds in that fashion; but since they say there are three kinds of evils, of one who is pressed by all the evils of two kinds, so that all things in fortune are adverse, and his body is oppressed by all things and worn out with pains, shall we say that this man wants but a little toward the happy life, not to say toward the happiest?

For if the soul is heart, or blood, or brain, then surely, since it is body, it will perish with the rest of the body; if it is breath, it will perhaps be scattered; if fire, it will be quenched; if it is the harmony of Aristoxenus, it will be dissolved. What shall I say of Dicaearchus, who says the soul is nothing at all? On all these opinions, nothing after death can concern anyone; for sensation is lost together with life, and to one who does not feel there is nothing in any respect that can matter. The opinions of the rest bring hope — if perchance this delights you — that souls, when they have departed from their bodies, can come into heaven as into their own dwelling. — It does indeed delight me, and I should wish first that it be so, and then, even if it be not so, that I might still be persuaded of it. — What need, then, have you of our help? Can we outdo Plato in eloquence? Unroll his book on the soul with care: you will desire nothing further. — I have done so, by Hercules, and indeed more than once; but somehow, while I read, I assent; when I have laid down the book and begun to reflect by myself on the immortality of souls, all that assent slips away. — What?

Now too, on this third dread day, / With grim swoop, tearing me with his hooked talons, / Jove's minion mangles me with savage feeding. / Then, glutted and sated to the full on my rich liver, / He pours forth a vast cry and, soaring on high, / With feathered tail he fawns upon my blood. / But when the gnawed liver is renewed by swelling, / Then again, greedy, he betakes himself to his foul repasts. / Thus I feed this guardian of my mournful torment, / Which fouls me, living, with unending misery. / For, as you see, fettered by Jove's chains, / I cannot keep the dread bird from my breast.

The whole cause, then, lies in opinion — and that not of distress alone, but of all the other disturbances, which are four in kind, more in their parts. For since every disturbance is a motion of the mind either devoid of reason, or spurning reason, or not obeying reason, and this motion is roused, in two ways, by an opinion either of good or of evil, the four disturbances are equally distributed. For two arise from an opinion of good: of which the one, exultant pleasure, that is, joy elated beyond measure, from an opinion of some great good present; the other, desire, which may rightly be called lust too, which is an immoderate craving of an imagined great good, not obedient to reason —

Let it be understood, then, that, the opinions tossing themselves to and fro, a disturbance is always in motion, inconstantly and turbidly; but when this fervour and agitation of the mind has grown old and has settled, as it were, in the veins and marrow, then there will arise both a disease and a sickness and those aversions which are contrary to those diseases and sicknesses. These things which I speak differ among themselves in thought, but in fact are coupled, and they arise from lust and from joy. For when money has been coveted, and reason has not at once been applied, like a certain Socratic medicine, to heal that desire, the evil penetrates into the veins and clings in the inward parts, and there arises a disease and sickness, which, when inveterate, cannot be plucked out; and the name of that disease is avarice;

This is that which Theophrastus could not sustain. For when he had laid down that scourgings, torments, torturings, the overthrow of one's country, exiles, bereavements have great force toward living badly and wretchedly, he did not dare to speak loftily and amply, since he felt humbly and abjectly. How well, is not the question; consistently, at least, certainly. And so it is not my wont to reprehend the consequences, when you have granted the first points. But here this most elegant of all the philosophers and the most learned is not greatly reprehended when he says there are three kinds of goods, but he is harassed by all, first in that book which he wrote On the Happy Life, in which he disputes much why he who is tortured, who is racked, cannot be happy. In it he is even thought to say that the happy life does not climb onto the wheel — that is, a certain kind of torment among the Greeks. He does not say that anywhere at all, but what he does say comes to the same.

do you grant this — that either souls remain after death, or perish in death itself? — I grant it. — What, if they remain? — I allow them to be happy. — But if they perish? — That they are not wretched, since they do not even exist; for that we were forced by you to grant a little while ago. — How, then, or why do you say that death seems an evil to you, when it will either make us happy if our souls remain, or, if we lack sensation, at least not wretched?

Thus, bereft, I myself receive these anxious plagues, / Seeking in love of death an end to my ill; / But far from death I am driven back by the will of Jove, / And this ancient, doom-laden calamity, heaped up through ages of horror, / Is fixed upon my body; / From which there fall drops melted by the sun's heat, / Which drip without ceasing upon the rocks of Caucasus.\" We seem, then, scarcely able to say that a man so afflicted is not wretched — and, if now wretched, then surely pain is an evil. — You are still pleading my case; but this I shall see to presently;

these two kinds, then, exultant pleasure and lust, are disturbed by an opinion of goods, as the two remaining, fear and distress, by an opinion of evils. For fear too is an opinion of a great evil impending, and distress is an opinion of a great evil present — and indeed a fresh opinion of such an evil that it seems right to be anguished at it; and this is, that he who grieves thinks he ought to grieve. But against these disturbances, which folly lets loose and stirs up against the life of men like so many Furies, we must fight with all our strength and resources, if we wish to lead through tranquilly and quietly this span that is given to life. But the rest another time; now let us, if we can, drive off distress. Let that be our subject, since you said it seemed to you to befall the wise man — which I in no way think; for it is a foul thing, wretched, detestable, to be fled with all effort, with sails and oars, so to speak.

and likewise the other diseases — as the desire of glory, as woman-madness, that I may so call that which in Greek is called philogynia, and the rest of the diseases and sicknesses are born in like manner. But those things which are contrary to these are thought to be born from fear, as a hatred of women, such as is in the Misogynist of Atilius, as a hatred toward the whole race of men, which we have heard of Timon, who is called the Man-hater (misanthropos), as inhospitality is: all which sicknesses of the mind arise from a certain fear of those things which they flee and hate.

Can I, then, who have granted to him that bodily pains are among evils, that shipwrecks of fortune are among evils — can I be angry with him for saying that not all the good are happy, since on all the good those things can fall which he counts among evils? The same Theophrastus is harassed both in the books and in the schools of all the philosophers, because in his Callisthenes he praised that saying: \"Fortune rules life, not wisdom.\" They say that nothing was ever said by any philosopher more feeble. Rightly, indeed; but I understand that nothing could be said more consistent. For if there are so many goods in the body, so many outside the body in chance and fortune, is it not consonant that fortune, which is the mistress both of external things and of those pertaining to the body, should avail more than counsel?

— Set forth, then, if it is no trouble, first, if you can, that souls remain after death; then, if you fail in that — for it is hard — you will show that death is free from every evil. For this very thing I fear may be an evil: not, I say, to lack sensation, but to have to lack it. — As authorities for the view you wish to be upheld, we can use the best — which in all cases both ought to and is wont to have the greatest weight — and first of all the whole of antiquity, which, the nearer it stood to its origin and divine descent, the better, perhaps, it discerned those things that were true. And so this one belief was implanted in those men of old, whom Ennius calls the "ancients" (casci): that there is sensation in death, and that a man is not so blotted out by his departure from life as to perish utterly;

meanwhile, whence come those verses? For I do not recognize them. — I shall tell you, by Hercules; and rightly do you ask. Do you see that I abound in leisure? — What of that? — You were often, I suppose, when you were at Athens, in the schools of the philosophers. — Yes, and gladly too. — You noticed, then, that although no one of them was at that time very copious of speech, still verses were mingled by them into their discourse. — Yes, and many indeed by Dionysius the Stoic. — Well said. But he gave them out as if by dictation, with no choice, no elegance: whereas Philo would add both his own and chosen poems, and that in their place. And so, since I came to love this kind of senile declamation, I for my part use our own poets eagerly; but where they have failed me — for I have translated much from the Greek, that Latin discourse might lack no ornament in this kind of disputation. — But do you not see what mischief the poets bring?

For of what sort does that man seem to you, sprung of Tantalus, born of Pelops, who once, having got Hippodamia by marriage, her snatched from her father-in-law King Oenomaus —? He, indeed, was the great-grandson of Jupiter. And yet so cast down, so broken? \"Approach me not,\" he says, \"guests; stand there, lest my contagion or my shadow harm the good. So great a force of crime cleaves to my body.\" Will you, Thyestes, condemn yourself and rob yourself of the light because of the force of another's crime? What? Do you not think that son of the Sun unworthy of his own father's light? \"His eyes shrank back, his body wasted with leanness, tears with their moisture ate away his bloodless cheeks; amid the squalor of his face, his beard, bristling with filth and unshorn, darkens his breast, scaly with foulness.\" These ills, O most foolish Aeëtes, you yourself added to yourself; they were not present in those things which chance had brought upon you — and that an inveterate ill, when the swelling of the mind had subsided (but distress, as I shall show, lies in an opinion of a fresh evil); but you mourn, plainly, from longing for a kingdom, not for a daughter. For her you hated, and rightly perhaps; but you bore the loss of your kingdom with no even mind. And it is a shameless grief, that of one wearing himself out with mourning because it is not permitted him to command free men.

They define a sickness of the mind as a vehement opinion about a thing not to be sought, as though it were greatly to be sought, clinging and deeply implanted. But that which is born from aversion they thus define: a vehement opinion about a thing not to be fled, clinging and deeply implanted, as though it were to be fled; and this opinion is a judging that one knows what one does not know. And under sickness are placed certain such things: avarice, ambition, woman-madness, obstinacy, daintiness, drunkenness, gluttony, and any like things. But avarice is a vehement opinion about money, as though it were greatly to be sought, clinging and deeply implanted; and like it is the definition, of the same kind, of the rest.

Or do we prefer to imitate Epicurus? Who often says many things excellently; for how consistently and harmoniously he speaks, he does not trouble. He praises a slender diet. That, indeed, is for a philosopher; but if Socrates or Antisthenes said it, not he who said that the end of goods is pleasure. He denies that anyone can live pleasantly unless he live also honourably, wisely, and justly. Nothing weightier, nothing worthier of philosophy — unless he were referring this very thing, honourably, wisely, justly, to pleasure. What is better than: \"Scanty fortune comes upon the wise man\"? But does he say this, who, when he has called pain not only the greatest evil, but even the sole evil, can be oppressed in his whole body by the keenest pains at the very time when he most glories against fortune? Which same thing Metrodorus too says, in even better words:

and this may be understood from many other things, but above all from the law of the pontiffs and from the rites of sepulchres, which men endowed with the greatest abilities would neither have tended with such care, nor sanctioned the violation of with so inexpiable a religious awe, had it not been fixed in their minds that death is not a destruction wiping out and blotting out all things, but rather a kind of migration and change of life, which in famous men and women was wont to be a guide to heaven, while in the rest it was held to earth and yet remained.

They bring on the bravest men lamenting, they soften our minds; then they are so sweet that they are not only read but learned by heart. So, when to a bad domestic training and a shadowed, dainty life there are added the poets too, they unstring all the sinews of virtue. Rightly, then, are they cast out by Plato from that commonwealth which he imagined, when he was inquiring after the best morals and the best ordering of the state. But we, taught forsooth by Greece, read and learn these things from boyhood, and count this a liberal education and learning. — But why are we angry at the poets?

Dionysius, indeed, the tyrant, driven from Syracuse, taught boys at Corinth: to such a degree could he not be without command. And what was more shameless than Tarquin, who waged war with those who had not borne his pride? When he could not be restored to his kingdom by the arms of the Veientes nor of the Latins, he is said to have betaken himself to Cumae, and in that city to have been worn out by age and distress. Do you think, then, that this can happen to the wise man — that he be oppressed by distress, that is, by misery? For though every disturbance is misery, yet distress is a very torture-chamber. Lust has its ardour, exultant joy its levity, fear its abjectness, but distress has something greater — wasting, torment, affliction, foulness; it tears, it eats away the mind, and plainly destroys it. Unless we so strip this off as to cast it away, we cannot be free of misery.

The definitions of the aversions are of this sort: that inhospitality is a vehement opinion that a guest is greatly to be fled, and that clinging and deeply implanted; and likewise are defined both a hatred of women, as of Hippolytus, and, as of Timon, of the human race. And, to come to the likeness of bodily health, and to use that comparison sometimes — but more sparingly than the Stoics are wont: as some are more prone than others to certain diseases — and so we call certain men subject to colds, certain to gripes, not because they are so already, but because they often are — so some are prone to fear, others to another disturbance; whence in some there is said to be anxiety, whence the anxious, in others irascibility. Which differs from anger; and it is one thing to be irascible, another to be angry, as anxiety differs from anguish (for not all are anxious who are sometimes anguished, nor are those who are anxious always anguished), as there is a difference between drunkenness and the habit of drunkenness, and it is one thing to be a lover, another to be in love. And this proneness of some toward certain diseases extends widely; for it pertains to all disturbances;

\"I have forestalled you, Fortune,\" he says, \"and seized you, and barred all your approaches, so that you could not reach me.\" Excellently — if Aristo of Chios said it, or the Stoic Zeno, who counted nothing an evil save what was base; but you, Metrodorus, who have hidden every good in the inward parts and the marrow, and have defined the highest good to be contained in a firm disposition of the body and an assured hope of it — you have barred the approaches of Fortune? In what way? For of that good you can be despoiled even now. And yet by such sayings the unskilled are caught, and on account of such opinions the multitude of these men exists;

From this, and by the belief of our own people, Romulus dwells in heaven and passes his days with the gods, as Ennius said, assenting to the common report; and among the Greeks, and thence passed down to us and even as far as the Ocean, Hercules is held so great and so present a god; from this Liber, son of Semele, was born, and with the same celebrity of report the brothers, sons of Tyndareus, who are reported to have been not only helpers of the Roman people's victory in battles, but even messengers of it. What? Is not Ino, daughter of Cadmus, called Leucothea by the Greeks and held to be Matuta by ours? What? Is not nearly the whole of heaven — not to pursue more — filled with the human race?

There have been found teachers of virtue, philosophers, who would call pain the highest evil. But you, young man, when a little while ago you had said this seemed so to you, on being asked by me whether it were greater even than disgrace, fell from your opinion at a word. Ask this same question of Epicurus: he will say that a moderate pain is a greater evil than the greatest disgrace; for in disgrace itself there is no evil, unless pains follow upon it. What pain, then, follows Epicurus, when he says this very thing, that pain is the highest evil? No greater disgrace do I look for from a philosopher. Wherefore you have given me enough, in answering that disgrace seemed to you a greater evil than pain. For if you will hold to this very point, you will understand how much pain is to be resisted; nor is it so much to be asked whether pain is an evil, as that the mind is to be steeled for bearing pain. — The Stoics draw up their little arguments to prove that it is not an evil;

And this indeed is plain: that distress arises when something has so appeared that some great evil seems to be present and pressing. Epicurus, however, holds that an opinion of evil is by nature distress; so that whoever fixes his gaze on any greater evil, if he thinks it has befallen him, is forthwith in distress. The Cyrenaics think distress is effected not by every evil, but by an unhoped-for and unexpected one. That, indeed, is no small matter toward increasing distress: for all things sudden seem heavier. And so those words too are justly praised: \"I, when I begot them, knew then they would die, and for that I reared them. Moreover, when I sent them to Troy in defence of Greece, I knew I was sending them to deadly war, not to a banquet.\"

it appears also in many vices, but the thing has no name. Therefore men are called both envious and malevolent and lustful and timid and pitiful, because they are prone to those disturbances, not because they are always carried away. This proneness, then, each toward its own kind, let it be called, from the likeness of the body, a sickliness, provided it be understood as a proneness to sicken. But in good things — because some are fitter for certain goods — let it be named aptitude (facilitas); in evils, proneness, that it may signify a tendency to fall; in neither case let it have the former name. And as in the body there is disease, there is sickness, there is vice, so in the mind. They call disease a corruption of the whole body; sickness, a disease with weakness; vice, when the parts of the body are at variance among themselves, whence comes the crookedness of the limbs, distortion, deformity.

but it is the part of one disputing acutely to see, not what each man says, but what ought to be said by each. As in that very opinion which we have taken up in this disputation — we hold that all the good are always happy. Whom I shall call good is plain; for those equipped and adorned with all the virtues we call now wise, now good men. Let us see who are to be called happy.

Indeed, if I should set myself to search out ancient things and to dig out from them what the writers of Greece have handed down, those very gods who are accounted of the greater nations will be found to have set out from here into heaven. Inquire whose tombs are pointed out in Greece; call to mind, since you have been initiated, what is handed down in the mysteries: then at last you will understand how widely this extends. But those who had not yet learned that natural philosophy which men began to handle many years afterwards had persuaded themselves only of as much as they had come to know at nature's prompting; they did not grasp the reasons and causes of things, and were often moved by certain apparitions, and these especially by night, so that those who had departed from life seemed to them to be living.

as though the dispute were about a word and not about a thing. Why do you deceive me, Zeno? For when you deny altogether that to be an evil which seems to me dreadful, I am caught, and long to know how that which I should reckon most wretched is not even an evil. \"Nothing,\" he says, \"is an evil save what is base and vicious.\" You return to your trifles; for you do not take away the thing that vexed me. I know that pain is not wickedness; cease to teach me that: teach me this — that whether I feel pain or do not feel it makes no difference. \"Never,\" he says, \"does it make any difference at least to living happily, which rests in virtue alone; yet it is to be rejected.\" Why? \"It is harsh, contrary to Nature, hard to suffer, sorrowful, cruel.\"

This forethought, then, of future evils softens their coming, when you have seen them coming long before. And so among Euripides the words spoken by Theseus are praised; for it is permitted, as we often do, to turn them into Latin: \"For I, remembering what I had heard from a learned man, used to ponder with myself the miseries to come: either bitter death, or the sad flight of exile, or some weight of ill I ever pondered, that, if some calamity should chance to be brought in, no sudden care might rend me unprepared.\"

And so those two, disease and sickness, are begotten from a shaking and disturbance of the whole bodily health; but vice is discerned of itself, the health being entire. But in the mind we can separate disease from sickness only in thought; viciousness, however, is a disposition or affection, throughout the whole life inconstant and at variance with itself. So it comes about that in the one corruption of opinions disease and sickness are effected, in the other inconstancy and repugnance. For not every vice has equal dissensions: as the affection of those who are not far from wisdom is, indeed, discordant with itself, while it is foolish, but not distorted nor depraved. But diseases and sicknesses are parts of viciousness; whether disturbances are parts of the same is a question.

For my part, I think those who are in goods with no evil joined; nor is any other notion subjoined to this word, when we say \"happy,\" save a heaped-up embrace of goods, with all evils set apart. This virtue cannot attain, if there is anything good besides itself. For there will be present a certain crowd of evils, if we count those things evils: poverty, ignobility, lowliness, solitude, the loss of one's own, grave bodily pains, ruined health, weakness, blindness, the destruction of one's country, exile, slavery in fine. In these so many and so great things — and even more can befall — the wise man can be; for these chance brings in, which can fall upon the wise man. But if these are evils, who can guarantee that the wise man will always be happy, since he can be in all of them at one time?

And as this seems the strongest proof brought forward why we should believe that gods exist — that there is no race so savage, no man of all so brutish, whose mind has not been imbued with a belief in the gods (many hold wrong notions about the gods — for that is wont to come about through depraved custom — yet all judge that there is a divine power and nature; and this no conference of men or coming-together brought about, the belief was not confirmed by institutions nor by laws; but in every matter the agreement of all nations must be reckoned a law of nature) — who, then, is there who does not lament the death of his own first on this ground, that he thinks them bereft of the comforts of life? Take away this belief, and you will have taken away mourning. For no one grieves at his own discomfort: men feel pain, perhaps, and are troubled, but that mournful lamentation and grieving weeping comes from this, that we think the one we loved to be deprived of the comforts of life and to be aware of it. And this we feel so by nature's lead, with no reasoning, no instruction. But the greatest proof is that nature herself gives silent judgement on the immortality of souls, in that all men care, and care greatly, for what is to be after their death. A man "plants trees to profit another age," as Statius says in the Synephebi — with what aim, save that he too believes that ages to come concern him? Will, then, the careful farmer plant trees whose berry he himself will never look upon, and the great man not plant laws, institutions, a commonwealth? What does the begetting of children mean, what the propagation of one's name, what the adoptions of sons, what the care over wills, what the very monuments and epitaphs of tombs, save that we think upon the future too? — What?

Here is a wealth of words — that what we all call by the one word \"evil\" he can express in so many ways. You define pain to me, you do not abolish it, when you say it is harsh, contrary to Nature, scarcely to be borne and endured; nor do you lie; but you ought not to give way in fact while glorying in words. \"So long as nothing is good but the honourable, nothing evil but the base\" — this is to wish, not to teach; the other view is both better and truer: that all things Nature recoils from are among evils, all she welcomes among goods. Once this is laid down, and the contention about words removed, yet so far will that excel which these men rightly embrace — what we call the honourable, the right, the seemly, which we sometimes embrace too under the name of virtue — that all else besides, which are accounted goods of body and of fortune, will seem exceedingly small and slight; so that it is not even any evil; nor, if all of them were gathered into one place, would they be comparable with the evil of baseness.

But that which Theseus says he heard from a learned man, Euripides speaks of himself. For he had been a hearer of Anaxagoras, who, they say, when the death of his son was announced, said: \"I knew I had begotten a mortal.\" Which saying declares that these things are bitter to those by whom they have not been thought of beforehand. So this at least is not doubtful, that all things which are thought evils are heavier when unforeseen. And so, although this one thing does not produce the greatest distress, yet, since the foresight and preparation of the mind avails much toward lessening pain, let all human things be ever pondered by a man as human. And doubtless this is that surpassing and divine wisdom — to have human things deeply perceived and handled, to wonder at nothing when it has befallen, to think nothing, before it has happened, cannot happen. \"Wherefore everyone, when his affairs are most prosperous, then most of all ought to ponder with himself how he may bear adverse hardship. Returning from abroad, let him ever think with himself of perils, of losses, or a son's fault, or a wife's death, or a daughter's sickness — that these are common, lest any of them ever be new to his mind; whatever falls out beyond hope, let him count all that as gain.\" Therefore, since Terence, having taken this from philosophy, said it so aptly, shall not we, from whose springs it was drawn, both say it better and feel it more steadfastly?

For vices are abiding affections, but disturbances are moving ones, so that they cannot be parts of abiding affections. And as in evils the likeness of the body touches upon the nature of the mind, so in goods. For there are in the body things excellent — beauty, strength, health, firmness, swiftness; there are likewise in the mind. For as the tempering of the body, when those things of which we are composed agree among themselves, is called health, so it is called of the mind, when its judgements and opinions are in concord; and this is the virtue of the mind, which some say is temperance itself, others say is something obedient to the precepts of temperance and following it, having no form of its own; but whether it be this or that, it is in the wise man alone. But there is a certain soundness of mind which falls even to the foolish, when, by the cure and purging of physicians, the confusion of the mind is taken away.

I do not, then, readily grant either to my Brutus, or to our common masters, or to those ancients, Aristotle, Speusippus, Xenocrates, Polemo, that, since they count among evils the things which I enumerated above, they should also say the wise man is always happy. If this distinguished and beautiful title delights them, most worthy of Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, let them induce their minds to despise those things by whose splendour they are caught — strength, health, beauty, riches, offices, resources, glory — and to count for nothing those things which are contrary to these: then they will be able to profess with the clearest voice that they are terrified neither by the assault of fortune, nor by the opinion of the multitude, nor by pain, nor by poverty, and that all things are placed for them in themselves, and that there is nothing outside their own power which they count among goods.

Wherefore, if, as you granted at the outset, baseness is worse than pain, pain is plainly nothing. For so long as it shall seem to you base and unworthy of a man to groan, to wail, to lament, to be broken, to be unmanned by pain — so long as honour, as dignity, as decorum is present, and you, looking to these, restrain yourself — pain will surely yield to virtue and grow faint at the soul's resolve. For either there is no virtue, or all pain is to be despised. Will you have prudence to exist, without which not even any virtue can be conceived? What then? Will it suffer you to do anything to no purpose, and labour in vain? Or will temperance allow you to do anything without measure? Or can justice be cultivated by a man who, through the force of pain, betrays what was entrusted to him, gives up his accomplices, abandons many duties? What then? To fortitude and her companions — greatness of soul, gravity, patience, contempt of human things — how will you answer?

For this is that countenance, ever the same, which Xanthippe is said to have been wont to declare was in her husband Socrates: that she always saw him with the same look going out from home and returning. Nor indeed was that brow such as was that of the elder Marcus Crassus, who, Lucilius says, laughed but once in all his life, but a tranquil and serene one; for so we have been told. And rightly was his countenance always the same, since no change came over the mind, by which the countenance is fashioned. Wherefore I accept, for my part, from the Cyrenaics these arms against the chances and events of life, by which their oncoming assaults may be broken by long premeditation; and at the same time I judge that evil to be of opinion, not of nature; for if it were in the thing itself, why should things foreseen become lighter?

And as there is in the body a fit shaping of the limbs, with a certain sweetness of colour, and that is called beauty, so in the mind an evenness and steadiness of opinions and judgements, with a certain firmness and stability, following virtue or containing the very force of virtue, is called beauty. And likewise, by like words, the strength of the mind is named, like the strength and sinews and efficacy of the body. But the swiftness of the body is called speed, which same is held to be a praise of talent too, on account of the mind's running through many things in a short time. This is unlike in minds and in bodies: that healthy minds cannot be assailed by disease, but bodies can; but the body's afflictions can happen without fault, those of the mind not so, all of whose diseases and disturbances arise from a spurning of reason. And so they exist in men alone; for beasts do something like, but they do not fall into disturbances.

As it is, both to say these things, which are of some great and lofty man, and at the same time to count, as the crowd does, among evils and goods, can in no way be granted. Moved by which glory, Epicurus comes forward; to whom too — if it please the gods — the wise man seems always happy. He is caught by the dignity of this opinion, but he would never say it, if he listened to himself. For what is there that less agrees than that he who says that pain is either the highest or the sole evil should also think that the wise man will say \"how sweet this is!\" then, when he is tortured by pain? Philosophers, then, are not to be regarded from single utterances, but from the continuity and consistency of their thought.

do you doubt that a pattern of nature ought to be taken from each best nature? What nature, then, is better in the human race than that of those who think themselves born to help, protect, and preserve their fellow men? Hercules has departed to the gods: he would never have departed had he not, while he was among men, paved that road for himself. These are old things by now, and hallowed by the religion of all men: what do we think those many and great men in this commonwealth had in mind, who were slain for the commonwealth's sake? That their name should be bounded by the same limits as their life? No one ever, without a great hope of immortality, would offer himself to death for his country.

Will you, cast down and prostrate and deploring in a piteous voice, be told: \"O brave man!\"? Nay, in such a state, no one would call you even a man. Either fortitude, then, must be given up, or pain must be buried. — But do you know this, that if you should lose some of your Corinthian bronzes, you can have the rest of your furniture safe, but if you lose one virtue — though virtue cannot be lost; yet if you confess that you lack one, you will have none at all?

But there is on these same matters something that can be said more subtly, if first we have looked at the opinion of Epicurus. He holds that all must of necessity be in distress who think themselves to be in evils, whether those evils were foreseen and expected beforehand or have grown old. For neither, he says, are evils lessened by age nor made lighter by premeditation, and it is foolish even to meditate on a future evil, or perhaps one not even going to be: every evil is hateful enough when it has come; but he who has always thought that something adverse could happen, to him that becomes an everlasting evil; and if it is not even going to be, a voluntary misery is undertaken in vain; so a man is ever anguished, either by receiving or by thinking of an evil.

Between the keen and the dull, however, there is this difference: that men of talent, like Corinthian bronze toward rust, both fall into disease more slowly and recover more quickly, the dull not so. Nor indeed does the mind of a man of talent fall into every disease and disturbance; for there are not many savage and monstrous ones; but some have even a first appearance of humanity, as pity, distress, fear. But the sicknesses and diseases of minds are thought to be more difficult to pluck out than those highest vices which are contrary to the virtues. For, the diseases remaining, the vices can be removed, because they are not healed so quickly as those are removed.

You bring me to assent to you. But see lest your own consistency be missed. — In what manner, pray? — Because I lately read your fourth book On the Ends; in it you seemed to me, in disputing against Cato, to wish to show this — which to me at least is approved — that between Zeno and the Peripatetics there is nothing but a novelty of words. And if that is so, what reason is there why, if it be consonant with Zeno's system that there is force great enough in virtue toward living happily, it should not be permitted to the Peripatetics to say the same? For it is the thing, I think, that ought to be regarded, not the words.

Themistocles might have lived at leisure, Epaminondas might, and — not to seek old and foreign examples — I myself might; but somehow there clings in our minds, as it were, a certain foreboding of ages to come, and this both arises most strongly and appears most readily in the greatest geniuses and the loftiest souls. Take this away, and who would be so mad as to live ever amid toils and dangers?

Can you, then, call Philoctetes there a brave man, or great-souled, or patient, or grave, or one who despises human things —? But from you I had rather depart; yet he, surely, is not brave, who lies in a dripping cave, \"who with his wailing, complaint, groaning, and roaring, makes the mute place re-echo his tearful cries.\" I do not deny that pain is pain — for why else should fortitude be needed? — but I say it is overcome by endurance, if only there be some endurance; if there is none, why do we deck out philosophy, or why are we proud in her name? Pain pricks, or let it even stab: if you are unarmed, offer your throat; but if you are covered with the arms of Vulcan, that is, with fortitude, resist; for these arms, the guardian of your dignity, will forsake and desert you, unless you do so.

The lightening of distress he places in two things: in calling the mind away from thinking on its trouble, and in recalling it to the contemplation of pleasures. For he holds that the mind can obey reason and follow whither it leads. Reason, then, forbids it to gaze on troubles, draws it away from bitter thoughts, blunts its edge for contemplating miseries; and when it has sounded the retreat from these, it drives and urges it again to look upon and handle with the whole mind the various pleasures, with which he thinks the life of the wise man is filled, both by the memory of past ones and by the hope of those to come. These things I have said after our fashion; the Epicureans say them after theirs. But let us look at what they say; how, let us not mind.

You have those things which the Stoics dispute precisely concerning the disturbances, which they call logika, because they are reasoned out more subtly. From which, since my discourse has, as it were, sailed out from rough rocks, let us hold the course of the remaining disputation, provided I have said those things clearly enough for the obscurity of the matters. — Quite enough; but if anything is to be known more diligently, we shall inquire another time; now we await the sails, of which you just spoke, and the course.

You, indeed, deal with me by sealed documents and bear witness to what I once said or wrote. With others proceed in that manner, who dispute under imposed laws: we live for the day; whatever has struck our minds with probability, that we say; and so we alone are free. But yet, since we spoke a little before of consistency, I do not think the question must be raised in this place whether what pleased Zeno and his hearer Aristo be true — that only what is honourable is good — but, if it were so, then whether it were consonant that he should place this whole \"living happily\" in virtue alone.

I speak of leading men. What? Do not poets too wish to be ennobled after death? To begin with, they wrongly reprehend the premeditation of future things. For there is nothing that so blunts and lightens distress as the perpetual thought, throughout all life, that there is nothing that cannot happen; as the meditation on the human condition, the law of life, and the practice of obeying it; which brings about not that we ever mourn, but that we never do. For he who thinks on the nature of things, on the variety of life, on the weakness of the human race, does not mourn while he thinks on these, but then most of all discharges the office of wisdom: for he attains both ends — that, in considering human things, he enjoys the proper office of philosophy, and that, in adverse chances, he is healed by a threefold consolation: first, that nothing befalls him save what he had long thought could befall, which thought alone most of all extenuates and dissolves all troubles; next, that he understands that human things are to be borne humanly; lastly, that he sees there is no evil save fault, and that there is no fault when that has happened which could not be warranted by a man.

Since, as in other places we have both spoken of virtue and must often speak — for most questions which pertain to life and morals are drawn from the fount of virtue — since, then, virtue is a constant and harmonious affection of the mind, making praiseworthy those in whom it is, and itself, of itself, by its own accord, praiseworthy even apart from any usefulness, from it proceed honourable wills, opinions, actions, and all right reason (although virtue itself can most briefly be called right reason). The contrary of this virtue, then, is viciousness — for so I prefer to call that which the Greeks call kakia, rather than malice (malitia); for malice is the name of a certain particular vice, viciousness of all — from which the disturbances are roused, which are, as we said a little before, the turbid and agitated motions of minds, turned away from reason and most hostile to a mind and life that is tranquil. There is some difference between toil and pain. They are altogether neighbours, yet still they differ somewhat. Toil is a certain performance, by mind or body, of a heavier task and duty; pain, on the other hand, is a harsh motion in the body, foreign to the senses. These two the Greeks — whose tongue is more copious than ours — call by one name. And so they call industrious men \"lovers of toil,\" or rather \"lovers of pain,\" while we, more conveniently, call them \"painstaking\": for it is one thing to toil, another to be in pain. O Greece, sometimes poor in words, though you always think yourself to abound in them! It is one thing, I say, to be in pain, another to toil. When Gaius Marius had his varicose veins cut, he was in pain; when he led his army under a great heat, he toiled. There is, however, a certain likeness between these: for the habit of toils makes the endurance of pains the easier.

And the same man so strains his keen vision on every side that he ever sees a seat and a place for living without trouble and anguish, so that, whatever chance fortune brings in, he bears it fitly and quietly. And a mind free of these makes men perfectly and absolutely happy; whereas the same mind, agitated and drawn away from sound and certain reason, loses not only steadfastness but even soundness. But even more easily can the force of nature herself be discerned in the beasts, because to them sense was given by nature. For some beasts she willed to be swimmers, the dwellers of the waters; others, winged, to enjoy the free heaven; some to be creeping, some to be walking; and of these themselves, part solitary-wandering, part gathered together; some savage, but certain ones tame; some hidden and covered by the earth. And each of these, keeping its own function, since it cannot pass over into the life of an unlike living creature, abides in the law of nature. And as to the beasts a different chief thing was given by nature to each, which each retains as its own and does not depart from it, so to man something far more excellent — although those things ought to be called excellent which have some comparison; but the human mind, plucked from the divine mind, can be compared with nothing else save with God himself, if this be lawful to say.

But why speak of these, to whom a victory at the Olympic games seems like that ancient consulship? Gladiators, either ruined men or barbarians — what blows they bear! Even when worn out with wounds, they send to their masters to ask what they wish: if their master is satisfied, they say they are willing to fall. What mean gladiator ever groaned, ever changed countenance? Which of them not only stood, but even fell, basely? Which, when he had fallen and was bidden take the steel, drew in his neck? So much do practice, training, and habit avail. Therefore a Samnite, a foul fellow, worthy of that life and station, will be able to do this; and shall a man born for glory have any part of his soul so soft that he cannot strengthen it by training and reason? The spectacle of gladiators is wont to seem to some cruel and inhuman, and perhaps it is so, as it is now conducted; but when guilty men fought it out with the sword, there could be, perhaps, many a lesson for the ears, but for the eyes none stronger, against pain and death.

But let us cast out altogether that chance concourse of smooth and round indivisible bodies, which Democritus nonetheless will have to be warmed and breathing, that is, animate. That soul, now, which — if it is of these four kinds, of which all things are said to consist — is composed of inflamed breath (as I see it seems best to Panaetius above all), must of necessity make for the upper regions. For these two kinds have nothing that bends downward, and ever seek the heights. Thus, whether they are scattered, this happens far from the earth, or whether they remain and keep their condition, all the more must they be borne to heaven, and by them be broken through and parted this thick and dense air which is nearest to the earth. For the soul is warmer, or rather more burning, than this air which I just now called thick and dense; and this can be known from the fact that our bodies, made up of the earthy kind of elements, are warmed by the heat of the soul.

That, indeed, is perhaps the greatest thing — to see the soul with the soul itself; and doubtless this is the force of Apollo's precept, by which he counsels each man to know himself. When, therefore, he says "Know thyself," he says this: "Know thy soul." For the body is, as it were, a vessel or a kind of receptacle of the soul; whatever is done by your soul is done by you. Which, unless it be done, the destruction of the virtues will follow. For into whomsoever distress falls, into the same it must of necessity fall to fear (for fear is an anxious expectation of future distress); but into whomsoever fear falls, into the same fall dread, timidity, panic, cowardice; therefore, that the same man be sometimes conquered, and think that that precept of Atreus does not pertain to him: \"Accordingly let them so prepare themselves in life that they know not how to be conquered.\" But this man will be conquered, as I said; and not only will be conquered, but will also be a slave; but we wish virtue ever free, ever unconquered; which, unless they are so, virtue is taken away.

But if the soul itself shall not know of what sort the soul is, tell me, I pray, will it not know even that it exists, nor that it is moved? From this arose that reasoning of Plato's, which was explained by Socrates in the Phaedrus, and which I set down in the sixth book of my Republic: "That which is ever moved is eternal; but that which imparts motion to something, and is itself stirred from elsewhere, must needs, when it has an end of motion, have an end of living. Only that, then, which moves itself, because it is never forsaken by itself, never even ceases to be moved; nay, for the rest of things that are moved, this is the source, this the first principle of motion.

But Gaius Marius, a countryman, yet plainly a man — when his veins were being cut, as I said above — at first forbade himself to be bound; nor is anyone before Marius said to have been cut without being bound. And yet that the bite of pain was sharp, this same Marius showed; for he did not offer the other leg. So he both bore the pain like a man, and like a man refused to bear the greater without necessary cause. The whole matter, then, lies in this: that you command yourself. And I have shown what kind of commanding it is; and this reflection — what is most worthy of patience, of fortitude, of greatness of soul — not only restrains the mind, but also, in some way I know not, makes the very pain milder.

That this is so the days declare, which as they pass so soften it that, though the same evils remain, not only is distress lessened, but in most cases removed. Fortitude, then, is an affection of the mind obedient to the highest law in the enduring of things, or the preservation of a stable judgement in undergoing and repelling those things which seem dreadful, or a knowledge of dreadful things and their contraries, or of those wholly to be disregarded, preserving a stable judgement of those things; or, more briefly, as Chrysippus (for the former definitions were of Sphaerus, a man among the first in defining well, as the Stoics think; for they are altogether nearly all alike, but declare the common notions, one more, another less) — how, then, does Chrysippus? \"Fortitude,\" he says, \"is a knowledge of things to be endured, or an affection of the mind in suffering and enduring, obedient to the highest law, without fear.\" However much we may assail these men, as Carneades was wont, I fear they are the only philosophers. For which of those definitions does not open up our notion, which we all have of fortitude, covered and wrapped up? And if there is enough protection in virtue toward living well, there is enough also toward living happily; for there is certainly enough in virtue that we live bravely; if bravely, also that we live with great spirit, and indeed so that we be never terrified by anything and be ever unconquered. But of a first principle there is no origin; for from a first principle all things arise, while it itself can be born of nothing else; for that would not be a first principle which were begotten from elsewhere. And if it never arises, neither does it ever perish; for a first principle, once extinguished, will neither be reborn itself from another nor create another from itself, since all things must needs arise from a first principle. So it comes about that the source of motion is in that which is moved by itself; and this can neither be born nor die — else the whole heaven and all nature must collapse and come to a stand, nor gain any force by which, struck at the first, it might be moved. Since, then, it is plain that that is eternal which moves itself, who is there who would deny that this nature has been given to souls? For everything that is stirred by an outward impulse is soulless; but that which is animate is set in motion by an inner motion of its own; for this is the proper nature and power of the soul. For at such a time we have nearly this ready: that nothing ought to seem unexpected. Or how shall he bear a misfortune more tolerably who has learned that something of the kind must needs befall a man? For this discourse takes nothing from the very sum of the evil; it only brings this — that nothing has happened that ought not to have been thought of. But for an orator to be angry is least of all becoming; to feign it is not unbecoming. Do I seem to you to be angry then, when in pleadings I say something more keenly and vehemently? What? Do you think Aesopus ever acted angry, or that Accius wrote angry? Those things are acted excellently — and indeed better by the orator, if he is an orator, than by any actor — but they are acted gently and with a tranquil mind. Which, even of the best things, as those are which you bring forward, ought yet to be calm and tranquil. And to praise distress, the one most detestable thing — of what philosophers, pray, is that? But Afranius said aptly: \"Provided he grieve at something, let him grieve at whatever you please.\" For he said it of a ruined and dissolute youth, but we are inquiring about a steadfast and wise man. Nor, indeed, does a brave and wise man ever even groan, save perhaps to brace himself to firmness, as in the stadium runners cry out as loud as they can. Athletes do the same when they train; boxers, indeed, even when they strike their adversary, groan as they hurl their gauntlets — not because they feel pain or give way in spirit, but because, in pouring forth the voice, the whole body is tensed, and the blow comes the harder. What of those who wish to cry out more loudly? Is it enough for them to tense the sides, the throat, the tongue, from which we see the voice drawn out and poured forth? With the whole body and, as the saying is, with every nail they serve the straining of the voice.

But still, it is useful to emulate, to disparage, to pity. Why should you pity rather than bring help, if you can do it? Or can we not be liberal without pity? First, it has memory, and that an infinite one, of countless things. This Plato will have to be a recollection of a former life. For in that book which is entitled Meno, Socrates asks a certain little boy some questions of geometry about the measuring of a square. To these he answers as a boy would, and yet the questions are so easy that, answering step by step, he arrives at the same point as if he had learned geometry. From this Socrates wishes it to follow that to learn is nothing else than to recollect. This passage he explains far more carefully in that discourse which he held on the very day on which he departed from life; for he shows that anyone whatever, however ignorant of all things he may seem, declares, in answering one who questions him well, that he does not then learn those things, but recognizes them by recollection; and that it can in no way come to pass that from boyhood we should have so many notions of so many great matters implanted and, as it were, sealed up in our souls — which they call ennoiai — unless the soul, before it had entered into the body, had flourished in the knowledge of things.

By Hercules, I have seen Marcus Antonius, when he was pleading earnestly for himself under the Varian law, touch the ground with his knee. For as catapults of stones, and the other engines for hurling missiles, have the heavier discharges the more strongly they are strained and drawn back, so the voice, so a running, so a blow, is the heavier the more it is sent with strain. Since, then, the force of this straining is so great, if a groan in pain shall avail to brace the mind, we shall use it; but if that groan be lamentable, if feeble, if abject, if tearful, the man who gives himself up to it I should scarcely call a man. And indeed, if such a groan brought any relief, still we might consider what was the part of a brave and spirited man; but since it lessens the pain not at all, why do we choose to be base to no purpose? For thirty-eight years Dionysius was tyrant of the Syracusans, having seized the dominion when twenty-five years old. With what beauty, with what resources endowed, did he hold a state oppressed by servitude! And yet of this man we have received it thus written by good authorities, that there was in his manner of living the greatest temperance, and that in conducting affairs he was a keen and industrious man, but the same malicious by nature and unjust; from which it must of necessity seem, to all who well behold the truth, that he was most wretched. For those very things which he had coveted he did not attain even then, when he thought he could do all things.

And since nothing is (as Plato everywhere argues — for he thinks nothing exists which arises and perishes, and that that alone exists which is ever such as it is: he calls it idea, we species) — the soul, shut up in the body, could not recognize these things, but brought a knowledge of them with it; whereby the wonder at the knowledge of so many things is taken away. Nor does the soul see them plainly when it has suddenly migrated into so unwonted and so disordered a dwelling; but when it has collected and recovered itself, then it recognizes them by recollection.

And this precept, which is given concerning pain, extends more widely: for against all things, not pain alone, we must resist with a like straining of the mind. To bear pain, then, calmly and quietly, it avails most to consider with the whole heart, as the saying is, how honourable a thing it is. For we are by nature, as I said before — for it must be said again — most zealous and most desirous of honour; and if we have caught, as it were, some gleam of it, there is nothing we are not ready to bear and to suffer, that we may attain it. And to me, indeed, it seems that nearly the same thing befalls those who meditate beforehand as those whom the days heal — save that a certain reasoning heals the one, while Nature herself heals the other, when that has been understood which contains the matter: that the evil which had been thought greatest is by no means so great that it can overturn a happy life.

But since I suspect that you are inquiring not so much about the wise man as about yourself — for him you think free of every disturbance, yourself you wish to be — let us see how great are the remedies which philosophy applies to the diseases of minds. For there is, certainly, a certain medicine; nor was nature so hostile and inimical to the human race that, having found so many healthful things for bodies, she found none for minds; toward which she has even deserved better in this — that the aids of bodies are applied from without, while the health of minds is enclosed in those very minds. But concerning the knowledge of the soul we cannot doubt — unless we are utterly leaden in natural philosophy — that there is nothing mixed in souls, nothing compounded, nothing coupled, nothing cemented together, nothing twofold: and since this is so, surely it can neither be sundered, nor divided, nor torn apart, nor drawn asunder, nor, therefore, can it perish. The Stoics, however, grant us a tenancy, as it were, like that of crows: they say that souls will abide long, but deny that they abide forever. Will you not, then, hear why, even if it be so, death is nonetheless not among evils? — As you please; but no one will dislodge me from immortality. — I praise that, indeed, though one ought not to be too confident in anything;

The first medicine in consolations, then, will be to teach that the evil is either no evil or a very small one; the second, both about the common condition of life and properly, if there be anything to be argued about him who mourns; the third, that it is the greatest folly to be worn out by mourning in vain, when you understand that nothing can be gained. For Cleanthes, indeed, consoles the wise man, who has no need of consolation. For if you have persuaded a mourner that nothing is an evil which is not base, you will have taken from him not his grief but his folly; and that is an unfit time for teaching. And yet Cleanthes does not seem to me to have sufficiently seen this — that distress can sometimes be taken up from that very thing which Cleanthes himself confesses to be the highest evil. For what shall we say, when Socrates had persuaded Alcibiades, as we have heard, that he was no real man, and that there was no difference between Alcibiades, born in the highest station, and any porter, and when Alcibiades, afflicting himself and weeping, was a suppliant to Socrates, that he would impart virtue to him and drive off baseness — what shall we say, Cleanthes? Was there then no evil in that thing which was affecting Alcibiades with distress?

\"What man anywhere among the nations has surpassed you in shamelessness? And who in malice has surpassed you?\" — you know what follows; for in alternate verses the gravest insults are hurled between the brothers, so that it readily appears that they are the sons of Atreus, of him who plots a new punishment against his brother: \"A greater mass for me, a greater evil must be mixed, that I may crush and press down that man's bitter heart.\" Whither, then, does this mass burst out? Hear Thyestes: \"My very brother urges me, wretched, to chew my own children with my jaws\" — he sets their flesh before him. For what is there to which anger does not advance, to the same point as fury? And so we properly say that angry men have gone out of their power, that is, out of counsel, out of reason, out of mind; for the power of these ought to be over the whole mind.

To this, then, shall virtue give way; to this shall the happy life of the wise and steadfast man yield? How base, O good gods! Spartan boys do not groan, mangled by the pain of the scourge. We ourselves have seen at Lacedaemon troops of young men contending with incredible effort with fists, heels, nails, finally with biting, so that they fainted before they would confess themselves conquered. What barbarian land is wilder than India or more uncouth? Yet in that nation, first, those who are held wise pass their lives naked, and endure the snows of Caucasus and the force of winter without pain, and, when they have applied themselves to the flame, are burned without a groan.

for we are often moved by something shrewdly concluded, and we waver and change our opinion even in clearer matters; for in these there is some obscurity. If that, then, should happen, let us be armed. — By all means; but I shall take care that it does not happen. — Is there any reason, then, why we should not dismiss our friends the Stoics? — I mean those who say that souls remain when they have departed from the body, but not forever. — Yes, dismiss those who undertake what is hardest in this whole case — that the soul can remain void of the body — but the other point, which is not only easy to believe, but, that being granted which they wish, follows from it, that very point they do not grant: namely that, when it has long remained, it should not perish.

What? Of what sort are those words of Lyco? Who, extenuating distress, says that it is moved by small things, by the discomforts of fortune and of the body, not by the evils of the mind. What then? Did that which Alcibiades grieved at not consist of evils and vices of the mind? Against Epicurus' consolation enough has been said before.

From these men either those against whom they try to make their assault must be withdrawn, while they collect themselves — but what is it to collect oneself but to gather the scattered parts of the mind again into their place? — or they must be asked and entreated that, if they have any power of avenging, they defer it to another time, while the anger cools. But to cool surely signifies an ardour of the mind roused against the will of reason. Whence is praised that saying of Archytas, who, when he had become rather angry with his bailiff, said: \"In what manner would I have treated you, had I not been angry!\"

But the women in India, when one of their husbands has died, come into a contest and judgement, whom he most loved — for several wives are wont to belong to single men; and she who is victress, joyful, is placed on the pyre together with her husband, her own people escorting her; she who is conquered departs in sorrow. Never would custom conquer nature; for nature is always unconquered; but we have infected the mind with shades, delights, leisure, languor, sloth, and have softened it, soothed with opinions and bad habit. Who is ignorant of the custom of the Egyptians? Whose minds, steeped in the errors of depravity, would sooner undergo any torture than violate an ibis, or an asp, or a cat, or a dog, or a crocodile; and even if they have done anything unawares, they refuse no penalty.

— You reprove them rightly, and the matter stands in that way. Shall we, then, believe Panaetius, when he dissents from his own Plato? For though everywhere he calls him divine, most wise, most holy, the Homer of philosophers, yet this one opinion of his, concerning the immortality of souls, he does not approve. For he holds — what no one denies — that whatever has been born perishes; and that souls are born, which the likeness of those who are begotten declares, a likeness that appears even in dispositions, not only in bodies. He brings, moreover, another reason: that there is nothing which feels pain but can also be sick; and that what falls into sickness will also perish; but souls feel pain, therefore they also perish.

Nor is that the firmest consolation, although it is both customary and often profits: \"This has not happened to you alone.\" It profits, indeed, as I said, but neither always nor with all; for there are those who reject it; but it matters how it is applied. For we must proclaim how each of those who bore wisely bore it, not by what discomfort each was affected. That of Chrysippus is, for truth, the firmest; for the time of distress, difficult. It is a great task to prove to a mourner that he mourns by his own judgement, and because he thinks he ought to do so. Doubtless, then, as in pleadings we do not always use the same \"status\" — for so we call the kinds of controversies — but accommodate it to the occasion, to the nature of the controversy, to the person, so, in lightening distress, we must see what cure each man can receive.
