Where, then, are those who say irascibility is useful — can madness be useful? — or natural? Or is anything according to nature which is done with reason resisting? But in what way, if anger were natural, would one be more irascible than another, or would the lust of avenging have an end before it was avenged, or would anyone repent of what he had done through anger? As we see King Alexander, who, when he had slain Clitus his friend, scarcely held his hands from himself; so great was the force of his repentance. These things being known, who is there who would doubt that this motion of the mind too is wholly a matter of opinion and voluntary? For who would doubt that the sicknesses of the mind, such as avarice, the desire of glory, arise from this — that that thing is greatly esteemed from which the mind sickens? Whence it ought to be understood that every disturbance too is in opinion.

I speak of men; but what? Do not the beasts endure cold, hunger, mountain-roving and woodland courses and rangings? Do they not so fight for their offspring that they take wounds, dread no assaults, no blows? I pass over what the ambitious endure and suffer for the sake of office, the eager for praise for the sake of glory, those inflamed with love for the sake of desire. Life is full of examples.

These things can be refuted: for they belong to one who is ignorant that, when we speak of the eternity of souls, it is the mind that is spoken of, which is ever free from all turbid motion, not those parts in which griefs, angers, and lusts are at work — which he, against whom these things are said, thinks set apart and divided from the mind. Again, the likeness appears more in beasts, whose souls are void of reason; but the likeness of men stands out more in the figure of their bodies, and it matters much to the souls themselves in what sort of body they are placed. For many things arise from the body which sharpen the mind, many which dull it. Aristotle indeed says that all men of genius are melancholic — so that I do not take it ill that I am rather slow. He enumerates many, and, as though it were established, brings a reason why this is so. But if there is so great a force toward the disposition of the mind in those things that are begotten in the body — and these, whatever they are, are what produce the likeness — the likeness brings no necessity at all why souls should be born. I pass over the unlikenesses.

But somehow or other my discourse has wandered from what was proposed by you. For you had inquired about the wise man, to whom either no evil can seem one, that is free of baseness, or so small an evil that it is overwhelmed by wisdom and scarcely appears; who adds and assumes nothing by opinion to his distress, and does not think it right that he be tortured to the utmost and worn out with mourning, than which nothing can be more depraved. Yet reason has taught — as it seems to me, at least — though this very thing was not properly inquired into at this time, whether there were any evil except what could also be called base, nevertheless, that we might see that whatever of evil there is in distress is not natural, but contracted by a voluntary judgement and an error of opinion.

And if confidence — that is, a firm trust of mind — is a certain knowledge and a grave opinion of one not rashly assenting, fear too is a distrust of an expected and impending evil; and if hope is the expectation of a good, fear must of necessity be the expectation of an evil. As fear, then, so the remaining disturbances are in evil. Therefore, as steadfastness is of knowledge, so disturbance is of error. But those who are said by nature to be irascible or pitiful or envious or anything of the kind, are constituted, as it were, with a bad health of mind, yet curable, as Socrates is said: when Zopyrus, who professed to discern each man's nature from his form, had collected many vices against him in an assembly, he was laughed at by the rest, who did not recognize those vices in Socrates, but was relieved by Socrates himself, who said that those vices were indeed born in him, but had been cast off by reason.

But let the discourse keep a measure and return whither it turned aside. The happy life, I say, will give itself to torments, and, having followed justice, temperance, and above all fortitude, greatness of soul, patience, when it has seen the face of the torturer, will halt, and, all the virtues having gone forth to torture without any terror of mind, will stand outside the doors, as I said before, and the threshold of the prison. For what is fouler than it, what more deformed, left alone, separated from that most beautiful company? Which, however, can in no way come about; for neither can the virtues hold together without the happy life, nor that without the virtues.

I could wish Panaetius were here — he lived with Africanus — that I might ask of him whose among his kin was that great-nephew of Africanus's brother like, who in face was like his father, but in life so like all the most abandoned men that he was easily the basest; like, also, the grandson of Publius Crassus, a man both wise and eloquent and foremost, and the grandsons and sons of many other famous men, whom it is needless to name. But what are we about? Have we forgotten that this is what we now proposed to ourselves — that, when we had said enough about eternity, even if souls should perish, there is no evil in death? — I had indeed remembered, but while you were speaking of eternity I gladly suffered you to wander from the proposal.

And there has been treated by us that kind of distress which alone is the greatest of all, so that, it being removed, we should think the remedies of the rest need not be greatly sought. For there are certain things wont to be said about poverty, certain things about a life unhonoured and inglorious; separately there are fixed schools on exile, on the destruction of one's country, on slavery, on weakness, on blindness, on every chance to which the name of calamity is wont to be given. These the Greeks distribute into single schools and single books; for they seek work — although the disputations, when full, are full of delight;

Therefore, as everyone endowed with the best health can seem by nature more prone to some disease, so one mind is more inclined to certain vices than another. But those who are said to be vicious not by nature, but by fault, their vices consist of false opinions of good and evil things, so that one is more prone than another to certain motions and disturbances. But an inveterate condition, as in bodies, is more troublesomely driven away than a disturbance, and a sudden swelling of the eyes is more quickly healed than a long-standing inflammation is driven off.

And so they will not suffer it to turn its back, and will snatch it with them, to whatever pain and torture they themselves shall be led. For it is proper to the wise man to do nothing of which he could repent, nothing against his will, to do all things splendidly, steadfastly, gravely, honourably; to expect nothing as though it would certainly come to pass; to wonder at nothing, when it has happened, as though it had happened unexpected and new; to refer all things to his own judgement, to stand by his own decisions. Than which what can be happier I certainly cannot conceive.

— I see that you look on high and wish to migrate into heaven. I hope it may be ours to attain it. But suppose, as those men will have it, that souls do not remain after death: I see that, if it be so, we are deprived of the hope of a happier life; but what evil does that opinion bring? For grant that the soul perishes as the body does: is there, then, any pain, or any sensation at all in the body after death? No one says that — though Epicurus charges it upon Democritus, the Democriteans deny it. Neither, then, does sensation remain in the soul; for the soul itself is nowhere. Where, then, is the evil, since there is no third thing? Is it because the very departure of the soul from the body does not come about without pain? Even if I should believe it to be so, how slight a thing it is! But I think it false, and for the most part it comes about without sensation, sometimes even with pleasure; and the whole thing is slight, whatever it be;

and yet, as physicians, in tending the whole body, heal even the smallest part if it has come to pain, so philosophy, when it has taken away distress in general, has taken it away too if any error has arisen from somewhere, if poverty has bitten, if disgrace has pricked, if exile has poured over any darkness, or if anything of those things I just named has arisen. Although there are proper consolations for single things, of which you indeed shall hear, when you will. But we must return to the same fountain: that all distress is far from the wise man, because it is empty, because it is taken up in vain, because it arises not from nature but from judgement, from opinion, from a certain invitation to grieve, when we have decreed that it ought so to be done.

But the cause of the disturbances being now known — which all arise from the judgements of opinions and from the will — let there now be a measure to this disputation. But we ought to know that, the limits of goods and evils being known, so far as they can be known by man, nothing greater or more useful can be sought from philosophy than these things which have been disputed by us in these four days. For, death being despised, and pain being lightened toward the enduring, we have joined the calming of distress, than which there is no greater evil for man. For although every disturbance of the mind is grave, and differs not much from madness, yet others, when they are in some disturbance either of fear or of joy or of desire, we are wont to call merely moved and disturbed, but those who have given themselves up to distress, wretched, afflicted, hardship-laden, calamitous.

The conclusion of the Stoics, indeed, is easy; who, since they have held that the end of goods is to agree with nature and to live in harmony with it, and since this is set in the wise man not only by duty but even by power, it must of necessity follow that, in whose power the highest good is, in the same man's life the happy life is. So it comes about that the life of the wise man is always happy. — You have what I think can be said most courageously about the happy life, and, as the matter now stands, unless you bring something better, even most truly. — I, indeed, can bring nothing better; but I would gladly obtain this of you, that, if it be not troublesome — since no bonds of any fixed school hinder you, and you take a sip from all, whatever most moves you by the appearance of truth — that which a little before you seemed to exhort the Peripatetics and the old Academy, that without retraction they should freely dare to say that the wise are always happiest, I should like to hear in what manner you think it consonant for these men to say this. For many things have been said by you against that opinion, and concluded by the system of the Stoics.

for it comes about in a point of time. What gnaws, or rather tortures, is the departure from all those things which are good in life. — See whether it may not more truly be said, from the evils. Why should I now lament the life of men? Truly and justly I might; but what need is there, when my aim is that we should not think we shall be wretched after death, to make life too more wretched by bewailing it? I did this in that book in which I consoled my very self, as much as I could. From evils, then, death takes us away, not from goods — if we seek the truth. And indeed this is so copiously argued by Hegesias the Cyrenaic that he is said to have been forbidden by King Ptolemy to say those things in the schools, because many, on hearing him, made away with themselves.

This being taken away, which is wholly voluntary, that mourning distress will be removed; yet a certain bite and a slight contraction of the mind will be left. Let them call this natural, by all means, so long as the name of distress be absent — grave, foul, baleful, which with wisdom can in no way exist or, so to speak, dwell. But what roots distress has, how many, how bitter! Which, the trunk itself being overturned, must all be plucked out, and, if it be necessary, by single disputations. For there is left to us this leisure, of whatever kind it is. But there is one principle of all distresses, many names. For both to envy is a part of distress, and to be jealous, and to disparage, and to pity, and to be anguished, to mourn, to grieve, to be afflicted with hardship, to lament, to be troubled, to feel pain, to be in trouble, to be afflicted, to despair.

And so it seems to have been done not by chance, but proposed by you with reason, that we should dispute separately about distress and about the other disturbances; for in it is the fount and head of miseries. But both of distress and of the remaining diseases of the mind there is one healing — that all are matters of opinion and voluntary, and are taken up for this reason, that it seems right so to do. This error, as it were the root of all evils, philosophy promises to draw out by the roots.

Let us use, then, the liberty which it is permitted to us alone to use in philosophy, whose discourse itself judges nothing, but is held forth on all sides, so that it can, by itself, of itself, no authority being joined, be judged by others. And since you seem to wish this, that, whatever be the opinion of the dissenting philosophers about the ends, yet virtue have enough of protection toward the happy life — which indeed we have heard Carneades was wont to dispute, but he as against the Stoics, whom he always most zealously refuted, and against whose teaching his talent had blazed up; we, indeed, will deal with that in peace — for if the Stoics have rightly laid down the end of goods, the matter is finished: the wise man must of necessity always be happy —

There is, moreover, that epigram of Callimachus upon Theombrotus of Ambracia, who, he says, though nothing adverse had befallen him, cast himself from the wall into the sea, after reading a book of Plato. But there is a book by that Hegesias I mentioned, the Apokarteron ("The Man Starving Himself to Death"), in which a man departing from life by abstinence is called back by his friends; answering whom, he enumerates the discomforts of human life. I could do the same — though less than he, who thinks it expedient for no one at all to live. I pass over others: is it even expedient for us? We who, bereft of both our domestic and our public comforts and adornments, surely, had we perished earlier, death would have drawn us away from evils, not from goods.

All these the Stoics define, and those words which I have named are of single things, and do not, as they seem, signify the same things, but differ somewhat; which we shall perhaps treat in another place. These are those fibres of the roots which I spoke of at the outset, to be pursued and all plucked out, that none may ever be able to arise. A great work and difficult, who denies it? But what glorious thing is not likewise arduous? Yet philosophy professes that she will accomplish it, if only we receive her cure. But these things, indeed, thus far; the rest, as often as you will, shall be ready for you, both in this place and in others.

Let us, then, give ourselves to her to be cultivated, and suffer ourselves to be healed. For, these evils sitting within, we can be not only not happy, but not even sound. Either, then, let us deny that anything is accomplished by reason, when, on the contrary, nothing can be done rightly without reason; or, since philosophy consists in the bringing together of reasonings, let us, if we wish to be both good and happy, seek from her all the aids and helps of living well and happily.

but let us inquire into each several opinion of the rest, if it can be done, that this glorious, as it were, decree of the happy life may be able to suit the opinions and teachings of all. But these, as I think, are the opinions about the ends that have been held and defended: first, four simple ones — nothing good save the honourable, as the Stoics; nothing good save pleasure, as Epicurus; nothing good save freedom from pain, as Hieronymus; nothing good save to enjoy the first goods of nature, either all or the greatest, as Carneades used to argue against the Stoics.

Let there be, then, someone who has no evil, who has received no wound from fortune: that famous Metellus, with his four honoured sons, or Priam with his fifty, of whom seventeen were born of his lawful wife; in both fortune had the same power, but she used it in the one. For Metellus his many sons and daughters, grandsons and granddaughters, laid upon the pyre; Priam, bereft of so great an offspring, when he had fled to the altar, an enemy's hand slew. Had he, with his sons living and his kingdom safe, perished — "amid embossed and panelled roofs, with barbaric wealth standing by" — would he then have departed from goods or from evils? Then assuredly he would seem to have departed from goods. But certainly it would have fallen out better for him, nor would those things be sung so tearfully: "All these things I saw set aflame, Priam's life by violence reft away, Jove's altar fouled with blood." As though, forsooth, anything better could then have befallen him by that violence! But had he perished earlier, he would have escaped that issue altogether; as it was, at that time he lost the sensation of his evils.

These, then, are the simple ones; the following, mixed: three kinds of goods, the greatest of the mind, the second of the body, the external the third, as the Peripatetics, and not much otherwise the old Academics; Dinomachus and Callipho coupled pleasure with honour, but Diodorus the Peripatetic joined freedom from pain to honour. These are the opinions that have some stability; for those of Aristo, Pyrrho, Erillus, and certain others have vanished. Let us see what these can maintain, leaving aside the Stoics, whose opinion I seem to have defended sufficiently. And the cause of the Peripatetics, indeed, is unfolded, except for Theophrastus and any who, having followed him, too weakly dread and shrink from pain; the rest, indeed, are permitted to do what they generally do — to exaggerate the gravity and dignity of virtue. Which, when they have raised it to heaven — as eloquent men are wont to do copiously — it is easy by comparison to grind down and despise the rest. For it is not permitted to those who say that praise is to be sought with pain to deny that those are happy who have attained it. For although they be in certain evils, yet this name \"happy\" extends far and wide.

For our friend Pompeius, when he was grievously sick at Naples, things took a turn for the better. The Neapolitans were crowned with garlands, and so, no doubt, were the Puteolans; from the towns the people offered public congratulations — a silly business, surely, and a bit Greekish, but fortunate nonetheless. Whether, then, had he been extinguished at that time, would he have departed from good things or from evil ones? Certainly from wretched ones. For he would not have waged war with his father-in-law; he would not have taken up arms unprepared; he would not have left his home; he would not have fled from Italy; he would not, his army lost, have fallen, defenceless, upon the sword and hands of slaves; his children would not have been mourned, nor all his fortunes possessed by the victors. He who, had he met death then, would have died amid the amplest fortunes — by the prolonging of his life how many, how great, how incredible calamities he drained! These things are escaped by death, even if they have not come to pass; yet, because they can come to pass — but men do not reflect that these things can befall them: each man hopes for the fortune of Metellus for himself, just as though either the fortunate were more in number than the unhappy, or there were anything certain in human affairs, or to hope were wiser than to fear. But grant even this very thing — that men are deprived by death of good things:

For as a trade is called profitable, a ploughing fruitful, not if the one is always free of all loss, the other of all calamity of weather, but if in each by a much greater part the gain stands out, so a life can rightly be called happy, not only if it is filled with goods on every side, but if by a much greater and weightier part the goods preponderate.

do the dead, then, also lack the comforts of life, and is this wretched? Surely they must say so. But can he who does not exist lack anything at all? For the very word "to lack" is a sad one, because this notion underlies it: he had, he has not; he longs for, seeks again, is in want. These, I suppose, are the discomforts of one who lacks: he lacks eyes — hateful blindness; children — childlessness. This holds among the living; but of the dead not only does no one lack the comforts of life, but not even life itself. I speak of the dead, who do not exist: do we, who do exist, lack horns or wings? Would anyone say so? Surely no one. Why so? Because, when you do not have a thing which is fitted to you neither by use nor by nature, you do not "lack" it, even if you feel that you do not have it.

There will follow, then, by the reasoning of these men, the happy life along with virtue even to punishment, and with it will go down into the bull, on the authority of Aristotle, Xenocrates, Speusippus, Polemo, nor will it, corrupted by threats or blandishments, desert it. The same will be the opinion of Callipho and Diodorus, each of whom so embraces honour that he holds that all things which are without it are to be set far behind. The rest seem to hold themselves more narrowly, yet they swim out — Epicurus, Hieronymus, and any who care to defend that deserted Carneadean end; for there is none of them who does not think the mind the judge of goods, and train it so that it can despise those things which seem good or bad.

This must be pressed again and again and urged home, once that point is firmly established about which, if souls are mortal, we cannot doubt — namely, that so great a destruction is in death that not even the slightest trace of sensation is left. This, then, being well settled and fixed, that other point must be shaken out, so that it may be known what "to lack" is, lest some remnant of error be left in the word. "To lack," then, signifies this: to be without that which you would wish to have; for there is willing inherent in lacking — except when it is said in some other sense of the word, as in a fever. For it is said in another way too: to lack, when you do not have a thing and feel that you do not have it, even though you bear it lightly. So "lacking" is not spoken of in death; for then there would be nothing to grieve at. That is spoken of: to lack a good, which is an evil. But not even a living man lacks a good, if he does not need it; yet in a living man it can still be understood that you "lack" a kingdom — though this cannot be said of you with sufficient nicety; it could be said of Tarquinius, when he was driven from his kingdom — but in a dead man it cannot even be understood. For "lacking" belongs to one who feels; and there is no sensation in the dead: therefore there is not even "lacking" in the dead. — And yet, what need is there to philosophize on this point, when we see that the matter has no great need of philosophy?

For the cause which seems to you Epicurus' will be the same of Hieronymus and Carneades, and, by Hercules, of all the rest. For who is too little prepared against death or pain? Let us begin, if you please, from him whom we call soft, whom we call given to pleasure. What? Does he seem to you to fear death or pain, who calls that day on which he dies happy, and, afflicted with the greatest pains, confutes those very pains by the memory and recollection of his own discoveries? Nor does he do this so that he seems, as it were, to babble off-hand. For of death he so judges, that, the living being dissolved, sense is extinguished, and that what lacks sense he judges pertains nothing to us. Likewise in pain he has fixed things which he follows, whose greatness he consoles by brevity, its long-continuance by lightness.

How often have not only our commanders, but whole armies as well, rushed to a death not doubtful! And if death were feared, Lucius Brutus would not have fallen in battle, barring the return of the tyrant whom he himself had expelled; the elder Decius, fighting with the Latins, his son with the Etruscans, his grandson with Pyrrhus, would not have flung themselves upon the enemy's weapons; Spain would not have seen the Scipios falling for their country in a single war, nor Cannae Paulus and Geminus, Venusia Marcellus, Litana Albinus, Lucania Gracchus. Is any one of these wretched today? Not even at that time, after his last breath; for no one can be wretched when sensation is destroyed.

How, at last, are those grandiloquent ones, against these two things which most cause anguish, better off than Epicurus? Or, as for the rest of the things that are thought evils, do not both Epicurus and the other philosophers seem sufficiently prepared? Who does not dread poverty? Yet not any of the philosophers. But this very man, with how little is he content! No one has said more about a slender diet. For indeed, the things which bring on the desire of money — that for love, for ambition, for daily expenses there may be resources at hand — since he is far from all these things, why should he greatly desire money, or rather why should he trouble about it at all?

"But this very thing is hateful — to be without sensation." Hateful, if it were "to lack"; but since it is plain that nothing can be in him who himself does not exist, what can there be hateful in him who neither lacks nor feels? — Although this point is made too often, yet that is because in it lies all the soul's contraction arising from the fear of death. For he who has sufficiently seen — what is clearer than the light — that, soul and body consumed and the whole living being destroyed and a universal perishing wrought, that living thing which once was has become nothing, will plainly perceive that there is no difference between the Hippocentaur, who never existed, and King Agamemnon, and that Marcus Camillus now cares no more about this civil war than I, while he was alive, cared about the capture of Rome. Why, then, should Camillus have grieved, had he thought these things would come to pass some three hundred and fifty years later, and why should I grieve, were I to think that, ten thousand years hence, some nation will get possession of our city? Because the love of country is so great that we measure it not by our own sensation, but by the safety of the country itself. And so death does not deter the wise man,

Or could Anacharsis the Scythian count money for nothing, and shall our own philosophers not be able to do it? A letter of his is reported in these words: \"Anacharsis to Hanno, greeting. My clothing is a Scythian covering, my footwear the hardened sole of my feet, my bed the earth, my relish hunger; I feed on milk, cheese, flesh. Wherefore you may come to me as to a quiet man. But those gifts in which you delight, give either to your fellow-citizens or to the immortal gods.\" Nearly all the philosophers of all the schools, save those whom a vicious nature had wrenched from right reason, could have been of this same mind.

death which, by reason of uncertain chances, hangs over us daily, and, by reason of the shortness of life, can never be far off — does not deter him from taking thought for the commonwealth and his own for all time, since he counts even posterity, of which he is to have no sensation, as concerning himself. Wherefore a man may, even while judging the soul to be mortal, set about eternal works — not from desire of glory, which he will not feel, but of virtue, which glory necessarily attends, even though you do not pursue it. But if nature is so constituted that, as our birth brings us the beginning of all things, so death brings the end — then, as nothing concerned us before our birth, so nothing will concern us after death. And in this what evil can there be, since death pertains neither to the living nor to the dead?

Socrates, when in a procession a great quantity of gold and silver was being carried, \"How many things,\" he said, \"I do not desire!\" Xenocrates, when envoys from Alexander had brought him fifty talents — which was the greatest sum of money in those times, especially at Athens — led the envoys to supper in the Academy; he set before them only what was enough, with no array. When the next day they asked him to whom he bade it be paid out, \"What?\" he said, \"did you not understand from yesterday's little supper that I have no need of money?\" When he saw them somewhat sadder, he accepted thirty minae, lest he seem to spurn the king's liberality.

The latter do not exist; the former it will not touch. Those who make death lighter would have it most like sleep: as though, forsooth, anyone would wish to live ninety years in such a way that, when he had completed sixty, he should sleep out the rest! Not even his own kin would wish that for him, much less he himself. Endymion, indeed — if we are willing to listen to fables — as he fell asleep, I know not when, on Latmos, a mountain of Caria, has not yet, I suppose, awakened. Do you think, then, that he cares when the Moon is in travail, by whom he is supposed to have been lulled to sleep, that she might kiss him sleeping? What should he care, who does not even feel? You have in sleep the image of death, and you put it on daily: and do you doubt that there is no sensation in death, when in its likeness you see there is no sensation?

But Diogenes, more freely, as a Cynic, to Alexander asking that he should say if he needed anything, \"For now, indeed,\" he said, \"a little out of the sun.\" Alexander had stood in the way of his sunning himself, doubtless. And this man was wont to dispute by how much he surpassed the King of the Persians in life and fortune: that to himself nothing was lacking, to that one nothing would ever be enough; that he did not desire those pleasures of which that one could never be satisfied, while his own that one could in no way attain. You see, I believe, how Epicurus divided the kinds of desires — not too subtly perhaps, yet usefully:

Let those follies, then, almost old wives' follies, be driven out — that to die before one's time is wretched. What time, pray? That of nature? But she, indeed, gave the use of life as of money, with no fixed day appointed. What, then, is there to complain of, if she demands it back when she will? For on that condition you had received it. The same men, if a little boy dies, think it must be borne with an even mind; if indeed in the cradle, that one must not even complain. And yet from this one nature has exacted more harshly what she had given. "He had not yet tasted," they say, "the sweetness of life"; but this one had already hoped for great things, which he had begun to enjoy. Yet in other matters it is thought better to attain some part than none: why otherwise in life? (Although Callimachus says, not amiss, that Priam wept far oftener than Troilus.) But the fortune of those who die at a full age is praised.

that some are natural and necessary, some natural and not necessary, some neither; that the necessary ones can be satisfied with almost nothing; for the riches of nature are easily got; but the second kind of desires he thinks is neither difficult of attainment nor of doing without; the third — because they were plainly empty, and touched neither necessity nor even nature — he thought must be cast out by the roots.

Why? For, I think, to none, were a longer life granted, could it be more pleasant; since surely nothing is sweeter to man than prudence, which old age, to take away all else, assuredly brings. But what age is long, or what is long at all for man? Has not old age, "following close behind, now boys, now youths in their course, overtaken them unawares"? But because we have nothing beyond, we call this long. All these things are called either long or short, just as each was given to each in due proportion. By the river Hypanis, which flows into the Pontus on the European side, Aristotle says certain little creatures are born which live a single day. Of these, then, the one that has died at the eighth hour has died at an advanced age; the one at sunset, decrepit — the more so if even on the day of the solstice. Compare our longest age with eternity: we shall be found in nearly the same brevity as those little creatures.

In this place many things are disputed by the Epicureans, and those pleasures are extenuated one by one, whose kinds they do not despise, yet do not seek their abundance. For they say that even the obscene pleasures, about which much discourse is held by them, are easy, common, set in the midst; and that these, if nature require them, are to be measured not by kind or place or rank, but by form, age, figure; and that to abstain from them is least of all difficult, if either health or duty or fame demand it; and that altogether this kind of pleasures is desirable, if it do no harm, but never profitable.

Let us, then, despise all follies — for what lighter name shall I impose on this lightness? — and let us place the whole power of living well in strength and greatness of soul, in the contempt and disdain of all human things, and in every virtue. For now, indeed, we are made effeminate by the softest reflections, so that, if death come before we have attained the promises of the Chaldaeans, we seem despoiled of certain great goods, deluded and forsaken.

And this whole matter of pleasure he so lays down, that he thinks pleasure itself, of itself, because it is pleasure, is always to be wished and sought, and by the same reasoning pain, for this very thing, because it is pain, is always to be fled; and so that the wise man will use this compensation, that he both flees pleasure, if it will produce a greater pain, and takes up pain producing a greater pleasure; and that all pleasant things, although they are judged by the sense of the body, are yet referred to the mind.

But if by waiting and longing we hang suspended in our minds, are tortured, are troubled — by the immortal gods, how pleasant ought that journey to be, when, once completed, no care, no anxiety will remain! How Theramenes delights me! How lofty is his spirit! For though we weep when we read it, yet that famous man dies not pitiably: who, when cast into prison by order of the Thirty tyrants, had drained the poison like a thirsty man, threw out the rest from the cup so that it rang, and at the sound thus made, smiling, said: "I drink this to the fair Critias" — who had been most foul toward him. For the Greeks are wont at their banquets to name the one to whom they are about to pass the cup. That excellent man jested with his last breath, when he already held the death conceived within his vitals, and truly foretold for him to whom he had drunk the poison's first draught that death which shortly followed. Who would praise this evenness of a most great soul in death itself, if he judged death an evil?

Wherefore the body rejoices so long as it feels present pleasure, but the mind both perceives the present along with the body, and foresees the coming, nor suffers the past to flow by. So that there will always be in the wise man perpetual and woven-together pleasures, when the expectation of hoped-for pleasures is joined with the memory of those perceived.

For Socrates goes into the same prison and, a few years later, to the same cup, by the same crime of judges as Theramenes had suffered from the tyrants. What, then, is that discourse which Plato makes him use before the judges when he had already been condemned to death? "A great hope holds me," he said, "O judges, that it goes well with me in being sent to death. For it must needs be one of two things: either that death takes away all sensation altogether, or that there is a migration from these places to some other place. Wherefore, whether sensation is extinguished and death is like that sleep which sometimes, even without the visions of dreams, brings a most peaceful rest — good gods, what gain it is to die! Or how many days can be found that are to be preferred to such a night! And if the whole continuance of all the time that follows is like it, who is happier than I?

And things like these are transferred to diet too, and the magnificence and expense of banquets is extenuated, because nature is content with a small refinement. For who does not see this — that all those things are seasoned by desires? Darius, in flight, when he had drunk water turbid and defiled with corpses, said that he had never drunk more pleasantly. He had never, doubtless, drunk thirsty. Nor had Ptolemy eaten hungry; to whom, when, roaming through Egypt, his companions not having followed, common bread was given in a hut, nothing seemed more pleasant than that bread. They say that Socrates, when he had walked rather vigorously till evening, and it had been asked of him why he did this, answered that he might sup the better — that he was buying up hunger by walking, as a relish.

But if those things are true which are said — that death is a migration to those shores which they who have departed from life inhabit — that is far happier still. To think that, when you have escaped from those who wish to be reckoned in the number of judges, you should come to those who are truly called judges — Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus — and meet with those who have lived justly and in good faith — can this journey seem to you a mean one? And to be permitted to converse with Orpheus, Musaeus, Homer, Hesiod — at how much, pray, do you value it? For my part, I would gladly die many times over, if it could be, that I might be permitted to behold the things I speak of. With what delight should I be affected when I met Palamedes, Ajax, and others circumvented by an unjust judgement! I should test, too, the wisdom of the highest king who led the great hosts to Troy, and of Ulysses and Sisyphus; nor, for inquiring into these things, as I did here, should I be condemned to death. — Do not you either, judges who have acquitted me, fear death.

What? Do we not see the diet of the Lacedaemonians in their common messes? Where, when the tyrant Dionysius had supped, he said that he was not delighted by that black broth which was the chief of the supper. Then he who had cooked it: \"No wonder; for the seasonings were lacking.\" \"What, pray?\" said he. \"Toil in the hunt, sweat, the run to the Eurotas, hunger, thirst. For with these things the feasts of the Lacedaemonians are seasoned.\" And this can be understood not only from the manner of men, but even from the beasts, which, whatever is thrown to them, provided it be not foreign to nature, are content with that and seek no more.

For no evil can befall any good man, living or dead, nor are his affairs ever neglected by the immortal gods, nor has this befallen me by chance. Nor indeed have I anything for which to be angry at those by whom I was accused or condemned, save that they thought to harm me." And these things in this manner; but nothing is better than the close: "But it is now time," he said, "to depart hence — I, that I may die; you, that you may live. But which is better, the immortal gods know; no man, I think, knows." Truly I would by no little prefer this man's spirit to the fortunes of all those who passed judgement upon him — even though that which he denies anyone save the gods to know, he himself knows, namely which is better; for he said so before; but he holds to the last that rule of his, to affirm nothing.

Certain whole states, taught by custom, delight in frugality, as we said a little before of the Lacedaemonians. The diet of the Persians is set forth by Xenophon, who says they apply nothing to their bread beyond cress. And yet, if nature should desire certain things even sweeter, how many things are begotten from the earth and the trees, both with easy abundance and with surpassing sweetness! Add the dryness which follows this continence in diet, add the soundness of health; compare those sweating, belching, stuffed with banquets like fat oxen:

But let us hold to this — that we judge nothing to be an evil which has been given by nature to all, and let us understand that, if death is an evil, it is an everlasting evil. For death seems to be the end of a wretched life; but if death is wretched, there can be no end. But why do I commemorate Socrates or Theramenes, men eminent in the renown of virtue and wisdom, when a certain Spartan, whose name has not even been recorded, so despised death that, when he was being led to it, condemned by the ephors, and was of cheerful and glad countenance, and a certain enemy had said to him, "Do you scorn the laws of Lycurgus?" he answered: "Nay, I owe him the greatest gratitude, who has punished me with a penalty which I can pay without borrowing and without a loan." O man worthy of Sparta! So that to me, at least, one of so great a spirit seems to have been condemned though innocent. Such men, past number, our own state has produced.

then you will understand that those who most pursue pleasure least attain it, and that the pleasantness of diet is in desire, not in satiety. They say that Timotheus, a famous man at Athens and a chief of the state, when he had supped at Plato's and had been greatly delighted with that banquet, and had seen him the next day, said: \"Your suppers, indeed, are pleasant not only at the time, but even on the next day.\" What of the fact that we cannot even use our mind rightly, filled with much food and drink? There is a glorious letter of Plato to the kinsmen of Dion, in which it is written nearly in these words: \"When I came thither, that happy life, which was talked of, full of Italian and Syracusan tables, in no way pleased me — to be filled twice a day, and never to pass the night alone, and the other things which accompany this life, in which no one will ever be made wise, and a temperate man much less. For what nature can be so wonderfully tempered?\"

But why should I name leaders and chiefs, when Cato writes that legions often set out eagerly to that place from which they did not think to return? With like spirit the Spartans fell at Thermopylae, on whom Simonides wrote: "Tell, stranger, that here you saw us lying at Sparta, while we obey the sacred laws of our country." What does that leader Leonidas say? "March on with brave hearts, Spartans; today, perhaps, we shall dine among the dead." This was a brave race, while the laws of Lycurgus were in vigour. One of them, when a Persian enemy had said boastfully in a parley, "You will not see the sun for the multitude of our javelins and arrows," replied: "In the shade, then, we shall fight."

In what manner, then, can a life be pleasant from which prudence is absent, from which moderation is absent? From which the error of Sardanapalus, the most opulent king of Syria, is recognized, who ordered to be cut on his tomb: \"These things I have which I have eaten, and which my sated lust has drained; but those many and glorious things are left lying behind.\" \"What else,\" said Aristotle, \"would you inscribe on the tomb of an ox, not of a king?\" He says that he, being dead, has those things which not even living he had longer than while he was enjoying them.

I commemorate men: what, pray, of that Spartan woman? Who, when she had sent her son into battle and heard that he was slain, said: "For this I had borne him, that there might be one who would not hesitate to meet death for his country." Be it so: brave and hard are the Spartans; the discipline of the state has great force. What? Do we not admire Theodorus of Cyrene, a philosopher of no mean repute? When King Lysimachus threatened him with the cross, he said: "Threaten, pray, those horrible things to your courtiers in purple: to Theodorus it makes no difference whether he rots on the ground or aloft." By which saying of his I am reminded to think that something must be said also about burial and the tomb — a matter not difficult, especially now that those things have been learned which were said a little before about feeling nothing. As to which, what Socrates indeed thought appears in that book in which he dies, of which we have already said so much.

Why, then, should riches be desired, or where does poverty not suffer men to be happy? You are eager, I suppose, for statues, for paintings. If there is anyone who delights in these, do not poor men enjoy them better than those who abound in them? For there is in our city the greatest abundance of all such things in public. Those who have them privately have neither so many, and rarely see them, when they have come to their country estates; and yet something pricks them, when they recollect whence they have them. The day would fail me, if I should wish to defend the cause of poverty. For the matter is plain, and daily Nature herself admonishes us with how few, how small, how cheap things she has need. Shall, then, ignobility or lowliness, or even popular disfavour, hinder the wise man from being happy?

For when he had discoursed of the immortality of souls, and the time of dying was already pressing, being asked by Crito how he wished to be buried, he said: "Much labour, my friends, have I spent in vain; for I have not persuaded our Crito that I shall fly away from here and leave nothing of myself behind. Nevertheless, Crito, if you can overtake me, or find me anywhere, bury me as shall seem good to you. But, believe me, none of you will overtake me, when I have departed hence." Excellently said by him, who both gave his friend leave and showed that he cared nothing about this whole matter.

See whether commendation to the crowd, and this glory which is sought, have not more of trouble than of pleasure. Trivial, indeed, was our Demosthenes, who said he was delighted by that whisper of a little woman carrying water — as is the custom in Greece — whispering to another: \"This is that famous Demosthenes.\" What is lighter than this? But how great an orator! Yet he had learned, doubtless, to speak before others, not much with himself.

Harder was Diogenes, who, though of the same mind, yet as a Cynic spoke more roughly: he ordered himself to be cast out unburied. Then his friends: "To the birds and beasts?" "By no means," he said, "but set a stick beside me, that I may drive them off." "How will you be able? for you will not feel." "What harm, then, will the mangling of beasts do me, who feel nothing?" Excellently Anaxagoras, who, when he was dying at Lampsacus, and his friends asked whether he wished to be carried, if anything should happen, to his homeland Clazomenae, said: "There is no need; for from every place the way to the world below is just as far." And on the whole question of burial, one thing must be held: that it pertains to the body, whether the soul has perished or is in vigour. And in the body it is plain that, whether the soul is extinguished or has slipped away, no sensation remains. But all things are full of errors.

It must be understood, then, that neither is popular glory to be sought of itself, nor ignobility to be dreaded. \"I came to Athens,\" said Democritus, \"and no one there recognized me\" — a steadfast and grave man, who glories that he was free of glory! Or shall pipers, and those who use the lyre, regulate their songs and measures by their own, not the multitude's, judgement, and shall the wise man, endowed with a much greater art, seek out, not what is most true, but what the crowd wishes? Or is anything more foolish than to think that those are anything in the mass, whom singly you would despise as labourers and barbarians? But he, indeed, will despise our ambitions and levities, and will reject the honours of the people even offered unasked; but we know not how to despise them before we begin to repent of them. There is in Heraclitus the physicist a saying about Hermodorus, chief of the Ephesians;

Achilles drags Hector, bound to his chariot: he thinks, I suppose, that Hector is being mangled and feels it. So he takes vengeance, as at least it seems to himself; but she mourns it as a most bitter thing: "I saw — what I most grievously endured to see — Hector dragged by the four-horse chariot." What Hector? Or how long will that be Hector? Better says Accius, with an Achilles for once wise: "Nay, in very truth I gave back the body to Priam; Hector I took away." It was not Hector, then, that you dragged, but the body that had been Hector's.

he says that all the Ephesians ought to be punished with death, because, when they expelled Hermodorus from the state, they spoke thus: \"Let no one of us excel; but if anyone shall stand out, let him be in another place and among others.\" Does not this happen so in every people? Do they not hate every surpassing of virtue? What? Aristides — for I prefer to bring forward Greek rather than our own examples — was he not expelled from his country for this cause, that he was just beyond measure? From how great troubles, then, are they free who have no dealings at all with the people! For what is sweeter than lettered leisure? — by letters I mean those by which we come to know the infinity of things and of nature, and, in this very world, the heaven, the lands, the seas. Honour, then, being despised, money too being despised, what is left that should be dreaded?

Lo, another arises from the earth, who will not let his mother sleep: "Mother, I call upon you, who relieve care suspended in sleep, and you pity me not — rise and bury your son!" When these things are chanted in subdued and tearful measures, which bring sorrow upon whole theatres, it is hard not to judge those wretched who are unburied. "Before the beasts and birds —" he fears lest he should make less good use of his mangled limbs; he does not dread their being burned. "Nor let him suffer the half-eaten remains, the bones laid bare, to be foully dragged through the earth, smeared with gore —" I do not understand what he fears, when he pours forth such good seven-foot lines to the flute. It must be held, then, that nothing is to be cared for after death, though many take vengeance even on dead enemies. Thyestes, in Ennius, curses in fine verses indeed, first that Atreus may perish by shipwreck: this is hard, surely; for such a death is not without grievous sensation; but these are empty: "Himself fixed upon the topmost rough rocks, disembowelled, hanging by the side, bespattering the rocks with gore, with corruption and black blood —"

Exile, I suppose, which is counted among the greatest evils. If that is an evil on account of the alien and offended will of the people, how that is to be despised has been said a little before. But if to be away from one's country is wretched, the provinces are full of wretched men, of whom very few return to their country.

the rocks themselves will not be more void of all sensation than that man hanging by the side, for whom he thinks to wish this torment. These things would be hard, if he felt; without sensation they are nothing. But this, indeed, is utterly empty: "Nor let him have a tomb to receive him, a haven for the body, where, human life laid aside, the body may rest from its ills." See in how great an error these things are involved: he thinks the dead man has a haven for his body and rests in the tomb. Great is the fault of Pelops, who did not instruct his son nor teach him how far each thing was to be cared for.

\"But exiles are fined of their goods.\" What then? Are too few things said about enduring poverty? But now, exile, if we seek the nature of the thing, not the ignominy of the name, how much, pray, does it differ from a perpetual sojourn abroad? In which the most noble philosophers spent their lives — Xenocrates, Crantor, Arcesilaus, Lacydes, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Antipater, Carneades, Clitomachus, Philo, Antiochus, Panaetius, Posidonius, and innumerable others, who, once having gone out, never returned home. But, you say, without ignominy. Can exile affect the wise man with ignominy? For all this discourse is about the wise man, to whom it cannot justly happen; for one justly exiled ought not to be consoled.

But why should I observe the opinions of individuals, when I may survey the various errors of nations? The Egyptians embalm their dead and keep them at home; the Persians even smear them with wax before burying, that the bodies may last as long as possible. It is the custom of the Magi not to bury the bodies of their own unless they have first been mangled by beasts; in Hyrcania the common people keep dogs at public expense, the nobles at their own: a noble breed of dogs, as we know; but each, according to his means, provides those by which he is to be mangled, and they think this the best burial. Chrysippus gathers very many other things, being, as he is, curious in all manner of lore; but some are so foul that speech shrinks and recoils from them. This whole topic, then, is to be despised in our own case, not neglected in the case of our own kin — yet so that we who live perceive that the bodies of the dead feel nothing;

Finally, toward all chances the reasoning of those is easiest who refer to pleasure the things which follow in life, so that, wherever this is supplied, there they can live happily. And so to every reasoning the saying of Teucer can be fitted: \"One's country is wherever it is well.\" Socrates, indeed, when he was asked of what country he said he was, answered \"of the world\"; for he reckoned himself an inhabitant and citizen of the whole world. What? Did not Titus Albucius, with a most even mind, philosophize as an exile at Athens? To whom, however, that very thing would not have happened, if, keeping quiet in public affairs, he had obeyed the laws of Epicurus.

but how much is to be granted to custom and report, let the living see to that, yet so that they understand it pertains nothing to the dead. But surely death is met with the most even mind when the dying man can console himself, as life ends, with his own praises. No one has lived too short a while who has perfectly discharged the duty of perfect virtue. For me myself there were many times fitting for death. Would that I had been able to meet it! For nothing more was being gained, the duties of life were heaped full, and only the contests with fortune remained. Wherefore, if reason itself accomplishes the less to make us able to neglect death, yet let a life well lived accomplish it, that we may seem to have lived enough and more than enough. For although sensation will have departed, yet the dead are not without their own and proper goods of praise and glory, although they do not feel them. For though glory has in itself nothing why it should be sought, yet it follows virtue like a shadow.

For how was Epicurus happier, because he lived in his country, than Metrodorus, because he lived at Athens? Or did Plato surpass Xenocrates, or Polemo Arcesilaus, in being happier? Of what worth, indeed, is that state to be esteemed, from which good and wise men are driven? Damaratus, indeed, the father of our King Tarquin, because he could not endure the tyrant Cypselus, fled from Corinth to Tarquinii, and there established his fortunes and begot children. Did he foolishly prefer the liberty of exile to servitude at home?

But the true judgement of the multitude about good men, if ever it is good, is more to be praised than they are happy on that account. I cannot say, however this is to be taken, that Lycurgus and Solon lack glory for their laws and public discipline, or Themistocles and Epaminondas for their warlike valour. For Neptune will sooner overwhelm Salamis itself than the memory of the trophy of Salamis, and Leuctra will sooner be removed from Boeotia than the glory of the battle of Leuctra. But far more slowly will fame forsake Curius, Fabricius, Calatinus, the two Scipios, the two Africani, Maximus, Marcellus, Paulus, Cato, Laelius, and others past number; and whoever has caught some likeness to these — measuring it not by popular fame but by the true praise of good men — will, with confident spirit, if so things shall fall out, advance to death, in which we have learned there is either the highest good or no evil. Nay, when his affairs are prosperous, he will even wish to die; for the heaping-up of goods cannot be so pleasant as their loss is grievous. This sentiment seems to be signified by that saying of the Spartan, who, when the Rhodian Diagoras, a famous Olympic victor, had on a single day seen his two sons crowned as victors at Olympia, came up to the old man and, congratulating him, said:

And now the motions of the mind, the anxieties and distresses, are soothed by forgetfulness, the minds being led over to pleasure. Not without cause, then, did Epicurus dare to say that the wise man is always in the more goods, because he is always in pleasures. From which that man thinks is effected what we seek — that the wise man is always happy.

"Die, Diagoras; for you are not going to ascend into heaven." Great things the Greeks think these, or rather thought them then; and he who said this to Diagoras, esteeming it a very great thing for three Olympic victors to come from one house, thought it useless to the man himself that he should linger longer in life, exposed to fortune. — But to you, indeed, I had answered, in few words, as it seemed to me, what was enough — for you had granted that the dead are in no evil — yet for this reason I strove to say more, because in longing and grief this is the greatest consolation. For we ought to bear with moderation the grief undertaken on our own account and for our own sake, lest we seem to love ourselves; but that suspicion tortures us with intolerable grief, if we imagine that those of whom we have been bereaved are, with some sensation, in those evils which the common run suppose. This opinion I wished to shake out of myself by the roots, and on that account I was perhaps the longer. — You, too long?

\"Even, if he shall lack the senses of the eyes, of the ears?\" Even so; for those very things he despises. For first, that dreadful blindness — of what pleasures, pray, is it deprived? Since some even dispute that the other pleasures dwell in the senses themselves, but those which are perceived by sight are not concerned with any pleasantness of the eyes, just as the things we taste, smell, touch, hear are concerned in that very part where we feel them. In the eyes nothing of the kind happens; the mind receives what we see. But the mind can be delighted in many and various ways, even though sight be not applied. For I speak of a learned and educated man, for whom to live is to think. But the thinking of the wise man does not generally call in the eyes as advocates for investigation.

Not for me, indeed. For the former part of your discourse made me wish to die, the latter sometimes not to be unwilling, sometimes not to trouble myself; but by the whole discourse this at least has been accomplished, that I should not reckon death among evils. — Do we, then, even desire the epilogue of the rhetoricians? Or do we now quite abandon this art? — Do not you abandon it, which you have always adorned, and rightly too; for, if we are willing to speak the truth, it had adorned you. But what, pray, is that epilogue? For I long to hear it, whatever it is.

For indeed, if night does not take away the happy life, why should a day like night take it away? For that saying of Antipater the Cyrenaic is, indeed, a little too obscene, but it is no absurd opinion; whose blindness, when little women lamented, \"What are you doing?\" he said; \"or does there seem to you to be no nocturnal pleasure?\" That old Appius, indeed, who was blind for many years, we understand, both from his magistracies and from his deeds, in that misfortune of his failed neither in his private nor in his public duty. We have heard that the house of Gaius Drusus was wont to be filled with those seeking advice; when those whose affair it was did not themselves see their own matters, they took the blind man as their guide. When we were boys, Gnaeus Aufidius, an ex-praetor, both gave his opinion in the senate, and did not fail his friends in their deliberations, and wrote a Greek history, and saw in letters.

— Men are wont in the schools to bring forward the judgements of the immortal gods concerning death — nor indeed do they invent these themselves, but on the authority of Herodotus and several others. First are proclaimed Cleobis and Biton, sons of the Argive priestess. The tale is well known. For when it was lawful for her to be carried in a car to a solemn and appointed sacrifice, at a place far enough from the town to the shrine, and the draught-animals delayed, then those youths whom I just named, having laid aside their garments and anointed their bodies with oil, went up to the yoke. So the priestess, carried to the shrine, the car having been drawn by her sons, is said to have prayed the goddess to give them, as a reward for their piety, that which is the greatest that can be given to man by a god; after which the young men, having feasted with their mother, gave themselves to sleep, and in the morning were found dead.

Diodotus the Stoic, blind, lived many years in our house. He, indeed — what would scarcely be believable — since he was engaged in philosophy even much more assiduously than before, and used the lyre after the manner of the Pythagoreans, and had books read to him night and day, in which studies he had no need of eyes — then, what scarcely seems possible to be done without eyes, he discharged the function of geometry, teaching his pupils in words from what point to what point they should draw each line. They say that Asclepiades, no ignoble Eretrian philosopher, when someone asked what his blindness had brought him, answered: that he was attended by one boy the more. For as even the utmost poverty would be tolerable, if it were permitted what some Greeks have daily, so blindness could easily be borne, if the supports of health be not lacking.

With a like prayer Trophonius and Agamedes are said to have prayed; who, when they had built a temple for Apollo at Delphi, worshipping the god, asked a reward — and no small one — for their work and labour: nothing definite, but whatever was best for man. To whom Apollo showed that he would give it on the third day after that day; and when that day dawned, they were found dead. The god judged, they say — and he indeed a god to whom the rest of the gods had granted that he should divine beyond all others. There is told, too, a certain little tale about Silenus; who, when he had been captured by Midas, is written to have given him this gift in return for his release: that he taught the king that the best thing by far for man is not to be born, and the next best, to die as soon as possible.

Democritus, his sight lost, could not, indeed, distinguish white from black; but yet good from bad, just from unjust, honourable from base, useful from useless, great from small he could; and without the variety of colours it was permitted to live happily, but without the knowledge of things it was not. And this man even thought that the keen edge of the mind is hindered by the sight of the eyes, and, while others often did not see what was before their feet, he travelled abroad into all infinity, so that he halted at no extremity. It is handed down too that Homer was blind; but we see his painting, not his poetry. What region, what coast, what place of Greece, what appearance and form of battle, what battle-line, what rowing, what motion of men, of beasts, is not so painted by him that he made us see the things which he himself did not see? What then? Do we think that either Homer or any learned man ever lacked delight of mind and pleasure?

Which sentiment Euripides used in his Cresphontes: "For it would befit us, gathering in throngs, to mourn the house where someone has been brought forth into the light, reckoning the various ills of human life; but him who has ended his grievous toils by death, him to escort forth with every praise and gladness, as friends." Something like this is in the Consolation of Crantor: for he says that a certain Elysius of Terina, when he was grievously mourning the death of his son, came to a place of consulting the dead, asking what had been the cause of so great a calamity; and that to him these three little verses of this kind were given on tablets: "Men err in life with minds unknowing: Euthynous won death by the will of the fates. Thus was it more profitable both for him and for you to be ended."

Or, if the matter were not so, would Anaxagoras, or this very Democritus, have left their fields and patrimonies, and given themselves with their whole mind to this divine delight of learning and inquiring? And so the augur Tiresias, whom the poets feign wise, they never bring on deploring his blindness; but Polyphemus, when Homer had feigned him monstrous and savage, he makes even talking with his ram and praising its fortunes, because it could go where it wished and touch what it wished. Rightly here, indeed; for the Cyclops himself was no whit more prudent than that ram.

Using these and like authorities, they affirm that the case has been judged by the immortal gods. Alcidamas, indeed, an ancient rhetorician among the most famous, even wrote a Praise of Death, which consists of an enumeration of human ills; he lacked those reasonings which are more nicely gathered by the philosophers, but he did not lack richness of speech. But glorious deaths met for one's country are wont to seem to the rhetoricians not only glorious but even blessed. They go back to Erechtheus, whose daughters too eagerly sought death for the life of the citizens; they commemorate Codrus, who flung himself into the midst of the enemy in a servant's garb, that he might not be recognized, had he been in royal array — because an oracle had been given that, if the king were slain, Athens would be victorious; Menoeceus is not passed over, who likewise, an oracle being delivered, lavished his blood upon his country; for Iphigenia at Aulis bids herself be led to be sacrificed, that the enemy be drawn forth by her blood. From there they come to nearer instances: Harmodius is on every lip and Aristogiton; the Spartan Leonidas, the Theban Epaminondas are in vigour. Our own men they do not know, whom it would be a great task to enumerate: so many are they whose deaths we see to have been desirable, with glory. Since this is so, must we nonetheless use great eloquence, and harangue as from a higher place, so that men may either begin to wish for death, or at least cease to fear it?

But in deafness, what evil is there? Marcus Crassus was somewhat deaf, but there was another more troublesome thing — that he heard ill of himself, even if, as it seemed to me, unjustly. Our people generally know not Greek, nor the Greeks Latin. Therefore these in the speech of those, and those in the speech of these, are deaf; and likewise all of us, in those tongues which we do not understand — which are innumerable — are surely deaf. But they do not hear the voice of the lyre-player. Nor even the screech of the saw, when it is sharpened, nor the grunt of a pig, when it is slaughtered, nor, when they wish to rest, the roar of the murmuring sea; and if songs by chance delight them, they ought first to consider that, before these were invented, many wise men lived happily; then that much greater pleasure can be perceived by reading these than by hearing them.

For if that last day brings not extinction but a change of place, what is more to be wished? But if it utterly destroys and blots out, what is better than to fall asleep amid the toils of life, and so, closing the eyes, to be lulled in everlasting sleep? And if this should be so, the saying of Ennius is better than that of Solon. For this poet of ours says: "Let no one honour me with tears, nor perform my funeral with weeping!" But that wise man: "Let not my death lack tears: let us leave to our friends mourning, that they may celebrate our funeral with lamentation."

Then, as a little before we led the blind over to the pleasure of the ears, so it is permitted to lead the deaf over to that of the eyes. For indeed, he who can converse with himself will not seek the conversation of another. Let all things be heaped into one, so that the same man be deprived both of eyes and ears, and be pressed besides by the keenest pains of the body. Which first, of themselves, generally make an end of a man; but if by chance, prolonged in length, they yet torture more vehemently than there is cause why they should be borne, what is there, at last, O good gods, that we should labour at? For a harbour is at hand, since death is in the same place, an eternal receptacle of feeling nothing.

But we, indeed, if any such thing should befall as to seem announced by a god, that we should depart from life, let us obey gladly and giving thanks, and think that we are being released from prison and freed from chains, that we may either sail back to our eternal and truly our own home, or be free of all sensation and trouble; but if nothing be announced, let us nonetheless be of such a mind as to count that dreadful day, dreadful to others, blessed to us, and to reckon nothing among evils which has been appointed either by the immortal gods or by Nature, the parent of all. For not at random nor by chance were we sown and created, but assuredly there was a certain power that took thought for the human race, and would not have begotten or nourished that which, when it had drained out all its toils, should then fall into the everlasting evil of death: let us rather think a haven and a refuge prepared for us.

Theodorus, to Lysimachus threatening death, said: \"A great thing, indeed, you have effected, if you have attained the force of a cantharis-beetle.\" Paulus, to Perses begging that he not be led in the triumph, said: \"That, indeed, is in your own power.\" Many things on the first day, when we inquired about death itself, not a few too on the next, when we dealt with pain, were said about death, which whoever recalls, there is surely no danger that he will not think death either to be wished, or at least not to be feared. To me, indeed, in the keeping of life that law seems best which obtains at the banquets of the Greeks: \"Let him either drink,\" it says, \"or depart.\" And rightly. For either let one enjoy the pleasure of drinking equally with the rest, or, lest, sober, he fall into the violence of the drunken, let him depart beforehand. So, by fleeing, you would leave behind the injuries of fortune which you cannot bear. These same things which Epicurus says, Hieronymus says in just as many words.

Would that it were permitted to sail thither with spread sails! But if we are driven back by contrary winds, yet we must needs be carried to the same place, only a little later. But what is necessary for all — can that be wretched for one alone? You have your epilogue, lest you should think anything passed over or left out. — I have indeed; and this epilogue, moreover, has made me the firmer. — Excellent, I say. But for now let us yield something to our health; tomorrow, however, and as many days as we shall be in the Tusculan villa, let us pursue these matters, and chiefly those which afford relief from distresses, terrors, and desires — which is the most plentiful fruit of all philosophy.

But if to those philosophers whose opinion is that virtue of itself is of no avail, and that everything which we call honourable and praiseworthy is, as they say, a hollow thing decked out with the empty sound of a word — if these men, nonetheless, think the wise man always happy, what, pray, ought to be done by the philosophers who set out from Socrates and Plato? Of whom some say there is such great excellence in the goods of the mind that by them the goods of the body and the external are overwhelmed; but others do not even count these latter goods, and place all in the mind.

Whose controversy Carneades was wont to judge, as it were, an honorary arbiter. For since whatever things seemed goods to the Peripatetics seemed the same advantages to the Stoics, and yet the Peripatetics attributed no more to riches, good health, and the rest of that kind than the Stoics did, since these things were weighed by the fact, not by words, he denied there was cause for disagreeing. Wherefore, in what manner the philosophers of the other schools can maintain this point, let them themselves see; to me, however, it is welcome that they profess something worthy of the voice of philosophers about the wise man's perpetual faculty of living well.

But since in the morning we must go, let us comprehend in memory these disputations of five days. I think, indeed, that I shall even write them out — for where can we better use this leisure, of whatever kind it is? — and we shall send these other five books to our Brutus, by whom we were not only impelled to philosophic writings, but even challenged. In which how much we shall profit the rest, I could not easily say; but for our own most bitter pains, and our various troubles poured around us on every side, no other relief could be found.
